positive_text:
Se tienen 2 cuadriláteros convexos congruentes de papel: $PQRS$ y $P'Q'R'S'$ ($PQ = P'Q'$, $QR = Q'R'$, $RS = R'S'$, $SP = S'P'$). Se corta el cuadrilátero $PQRS$ por la diagonal $PR$ y se corta el cuadrilátero $P'Q'R'S'$ por la diagonal $Q'S'$, obteniendo así cuatro trozos de papel.

a) Indica un procedimiento general, que funcione para cualquier cuadrilátero convexo $PQRS$, que permita formar un paralelogramo con los cuatro pedazos.

b) Si los lados de los cuadriláteros miden $3$, $3$, $4$ y $6$, demuestra que el perímetro del paralelogramo construido es mayor que $16$ y menor que $28$, independientemente del orden de los lados.

negatives.text:

a) Indica un procedimiento general que permita armar un triángulo con los cuatro pedazos de papel.

b) Si los lados de los cuadriláteros miden $3$, $3$, $4$ y $6$, demuestra que el perímetro del triángulo es mayor que $16$ y menor que $28$.

positive_text:
Sea $p > 3$ un número primo. Si
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{1}{k^2} = \frac{a}{b}
$$
donde $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, demuestre que $p^3$ divide a $a$.

negatives.text:
Sea $p > 3$ un número primo. Si
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{1}{k^3} = \frac{a}{b}
$$
donde $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, demuestre que $p^3$ divide a $a$.

Sea $p > 3$ un número primo. Si
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{p} \frac{1}{k^2} = \frac{a}{b}
$$
donde $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, demuestre que $p^3$ divide a $a$.

positive_text:
a) Para cada $k \ge 3$, encontrar un número natural $n$ tal que existan exactamente $k$ divisores positivos distintos de $n$ cuya suma es igual a $n$.

b) Supongamos que $n$ es la suma de $k$ divisores positivos distintos de $n$, para algún $k \ge 3$. Si $p$ es el número primo más pequeño que divide a $n$, probar que
$$
\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{p+k-1} \ge 1.
$$

negatives.text:
a) Para cada $k \ge 3$, hallar un entero positivo $n$ que se pueda representar como producto de exactamente $k$ divisores positivos de $n$ distintos entre sí.

b) Supongamos que $n$ se puede expresar como producto de exactamente $k$ divisores positivos de $n$ distintos entre sí, para algún $k \ge 3$. Sea $p$ el menor divisor primo de $n$.
Demostrar que
$$
\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{p+k-1} \ge 1.
$$

a) Para cada $k \ge 3$, hallar un entero positivo $n$ que se pueda representar como suma de exactamente $k$ divisores positivos de $n$ distintos entre sí, pero que no sean múltiplos entre sí.

b) Supongamos que $n$ se puede expresar como suma de exactamente $k$ divisores positivos de $n$ distintos entre sí, para algún $k \ge 3$. Sea $p$ el menor divisor primo de $n$.
Demostrar que
$$
\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{p+k-1} \ge 1.
$$

a) Para cada $k \ge 3$, hallar un entero positivo $n$ que se pueda representar como suma de exactamente $k$ divisores positivos de $n$ distintos entre sí, tales que su suma es estrictamente menor que $n$.

b) Supongamos que $n$ se puede expresar como suma de exactamente $k$ divisores positivos de $n$ distintos entre sí, para algún $k \ge 3$. Sea $p$ el menor divisor primo de $n$.
Demostrar que
$$
\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{p+k-1} \ge 1.
$$

positive_text: Sea $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ una sucesión infinita de enteros positivos que cumple con la relación de recurrencia $$ a_{n+2} = \gcd(a_{n+1}, a_n) + 2006, $$ para cada $n = 1, 2, \dots$. ¿Es posible que tal sucesión tenga exactamente $10^{2006}$ valores distintos?

negatives.text: Consideramos todas las sucesiones infinitas $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ de enteros positivos que satisfacen la recurrencia $$ x_{n+2} = \text{mcd}(x_{n+1}, x_n) - 2006, $$ para todo $n = 1, 2, \dots$. ¿Puede ocurrir que una sucesión de este tipo contenga exactamente $10^{2006}$ números distintos?

Consideramos todas las sucesiones infinitas $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ de enteros positivos que satisfacen la recurrencia $$ x_{n+2} = \text{mcd}(x_{n+1}, x_n)^2 + 2006, $$ para todo $n = 1, 2, \dots$. ¿Puede ocurrir que una sucesión de este tipo contenga exactamente $10^{2006}$ números distintos?

Consideramos todas las sucesiones infinitas $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ de enteros positivos que satisfacen la recurrencia $$ x_{n+2} = \text{mcd}(x_{n+1}, x_n) + 2006^2, $$ para todo $n = 1, 2, \dots$. ¿Puede ocurrir que una sucesión de este tipo contenga exactamente $10^{2006}$ números distintos?

positive_text: Sea $n$ un entero impar mayor o igual a $3$. En un conjunto de $n$ individuos, algunos siempre dicen la verdad (veraces) y los restantes no tienen comportamiento constante (impredecibles). Se conoce que el número de impredecibles es a lo más $(n-1)/2$. Un observador externo debe identificar a cada individuo mediante una serie de consultas. En cada consulta elige dos individuos $A$ y $B$ y pregunta a $A$ si $B$ es veraz. Demostrar que tras a lo sumo $\frac{3(n-1)}{2}$ consultas, el observador podrá identificar con certeza a todos los individuos.

negatives.text: Sea $k \ge 1$ un entero. En un grupo de $2k+1$ personas, algunas siempre dicen la verdad y las restantes siempre mienten. Se sabe que hay a lo sumo $k$ mentirosas. Alguien ajeno al grupo debe determinar quién es sincero y quién mentiroso mediante una secuencia de pasos. En cada paso elige dos personas $A$ y $B$ y le pregunta a $A$ si $B$ es sincera. Demostrar que al cabo de $3k$ pasos el forastero podrá clasificar con certeza a las $2k+1$ personas del grupo.

Sea $k \ge 1$ un entero. En un grupo de $2k+1$ personas, algunas siempre dicen la verdad y las restantes son impredecibles. Se sabe que las impredecibles son a lo sumo $k$. Alguien ajeno al grupo debe determinar quién es sincero y quién impredecible mediante una secuencia de pasos. En cada paso elige dos personas $A$ y $B$ y le pregunta a $A$ si $B$ es impredecible. Demostrar que al cabo de $3k$ pasos el forastero podrá clasificar con certeza a las $2k+1$ personas del grupo.

Sea $k \ge 1$ un entero. En un grupo de $2k+1$ personas, algunas siempre dicen la verdad y las restantes son impredecibles. Se sabe que las impredecibles son a lo sumo $k$. Alguien ajeno al grupo debe determinar quién es sincero y quién impredecible mediante una secuencia de pasos. En cada paso elige tres personas $A$, $B$ y $C$ y le pregunta a $A$ si $B$ y $C$ son sinceros. Demostrar que al cabo de $3k$ pasos el forastero podrá clasificar con certeza a las $2k+1$ personas del grupo.

positive_text:
Sea $m$ un entero positivo y considérese la sucesión $\{b_n\}$ definida por:
$$
b_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad b_{n+1} = b_n \cdot \lceil b_n \rceil, \text{ si } n \ge 1.
$$
Hallar todos los valores de $m$ tales que $b_{2007}$ es el primer término de la sucesión que es un número entero.
Nota: $\lceil x \rceil$ denota el menor entero mayor o igual a $x$.

negatives.text:
Dado un entero positivo $m$, se define la sucesión $\{c_n\}$ mediante:
$$
c_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad c_{n+1} = c_n [c_n] + 1, \text{ si } n \ge 1.
$$
Determinar todos los valores de $m$ para los cuales $c_{2007}$ es el primer entero que aparece en la sucesión.

Dado un entero positivo $m$, se define la sucesión $\{d_n\}$ mediante:
$$
d_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad d_{n+1} = d_n [d_n], \text{ si } n \ge 1.
$$
Determinar todos los valores de $m$ para los cuales $d_{2007}$ es el primer número irracional que aparece en la sucesión.

Dado un entero positivo $m$, se define la sucesión $\{e_n\}$ mediante:
$$
e_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad e_{n+1} = e_n \cdot \lfloor e_n \rfloor, \text{ si } n \ge 1.
$$
Determinar todos los valores de $m$ para los cuales $e_{2007}$ es el primer entero que aparece en la sucesión.

positive_text: Sea $n > 2$ un número par. En un tablero de $n \times n$, se colocan fichas de tal forma que cada columna contenga un número par estrictamente positivo de fichas y cada fila contenga un número impar de fichas. Determinar el mínimo número total de fichas necesarias para satisfacer estas condiciones. Exhibir una distribución que alcance este mínimo y justificar por qué es imposible obtenerlo con un número menor.

negatives.text: Sea $n > 2$ un número par. Determinar el mínimo número total de fichas necesarias para satisfacer estas condiciones.

positive_text: Dos jugadores, $X$ y $Y$, compiten por un círculo. $X$ dispone de $n$ marcas rojas y $Y$ de $n$ marcas verdes ($n \ge 2$). $X$ inicia el juego y ambos colocan una marca a la vez en posiciones distintas de la circunferencia. Una vez ubicadas las $2n$ marcas, cada punto del círculo se adjudica al jugador cuya marca esté más cerca. Si hay empate de distancias, el punto se declara neutro. Gana quien ocupe mayor área. Mostrar que, para cualquier $n$, $Y$ tiene estrategia para asegurar la victoria.

negatives.text: Dos equipos, $A$ y $B$, disputan el territorio limitado por una circunferencia. $A$ tiene $n$ banderas azules y $B$ tiene $n$ banderas blancas ($n \ge 2$). Juegan alternadamente y $A$ comienza. Cada equipo coloca una de sus banderas en un punto de la circunferencia no usado. Gana el equipo cuyas banderas estén más lejos, en promedio, de las banderas del otro equipo. Demostrar que $B$ tiene estrategia para ganar.

Dos equipos, $A$ y $B$, juegan en una circunferencia. $A$ tiene $n$ banderas azules y $B$ tiene $n$ banderas blancas ($n \ge 2$). $A$ comienza y colocan banderas en posiciones no usadas. Un punto es de $A$ si está más cerca de una bandera azul que de cualquier bandera blanca, y viceversa. Si hay empate, el punto es neutral. Gana $A$ si tiene al menos una bandera más cercana que $B$ a más de la mitad de los puntos. Demostrar que $B$ tiene estrategia para ganar.

positive_text: Un tablero rectangular de $m$ filas y $n$ columnas ($m \ge 2, n \ge 2$) debe ser completamente cubierto con piezas de dominó de tamaño $2 \times 1$, donde cada pieza tiene un cuadrado con el número $1$ y otro con el número $-1$. Las piezas no pueden superponerse ni salir del tablero. Se requiere que el producto de los números en cada fila sea negativo y el producto de los números en cada columna sea positivo. Determine para qué valores de $m$ y $n$ es posible hacer esto, y para tales valores, proporcione una configuración válida. En otros casos, justifique por qué es imposible.

negatives.text: Un tablero rectangular de $a$ filas y $b$ columnas ($a \ge 2, b \ge 2$) debe ser completamente cubierto con piezas de dominó de tamaño $2 \times 1$, donde cada pieza tiene un cuadrado con el número $1$ y otro con el número $-1$. positive_text: Sean $a$ y $b$ enteros tales que el polinomio $Q(x) = x^3 + a x + b$ satisface la siguiente propiedad: para enteros $u$ y $v$, si $107$ divide a $Q(u) - Q(v)$, entonces $107$ divide a $u - v$. Demuestre que $107$ divide a $a$.

negatives.text: Sean $m$ y $n$ enteros tales que el polinomio $P(x) = x^3 + m x + n$ tiene la siguiente propiedad: si $x$ e $y$ son enteros y $107$ divide a $P(x) + P(y)$, entonces $107$ divide a $x - y$. Demuestre que $107$ divide a $m$.

Sean $m$ y $n$ enteros tales que el polinomio $P(x) = x^3 + m x + n$ tiene la siguiente propiedad: si $x$ e $y$ son enteros y $107$ divide a $P(x) - P(y)$, entonces $107$ divide a $x + y$. Demuestre que $107$ divide a $m$.

Sean $m$ y $n$ enteros tales que el polinomio $P(x) = x^3 + m x + n$ tiene la siguiente propiedad: si $x$ e $y$ son enteros y $108$ divide a $P(x) - P(y)$, entonces $108$ divide a $x - y$. Demuestre que $108$ divide a $m$.

positive_text: Let $N \ge 4$ be a fixed integer. Two players $X$ and $Y$ take turns appending a number to a sequence. The players aim to ensure that at some point, a consecutive subsequence of the sequence has a total sum divisible by $N$. In the acute-angled triangle $ABP$ ($AB > BP$) the altitudes are $BH$, $PQ$, and $AS$. The extension of $QS$ intersects line $AP$ at $C$. The extension of $HS$ intersects $BC$ at $L$. If $HS = SL$ and $HL$ is perpendicular to $AC$, compute $\frac{SL}{SC}$.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)
$$
holds for all positive integers $a, b$ where the ratio $\frac{a}{b}$ lies in the interval $\left(10^6 - 10^{-6}, 10^6 + 10^{-6}\right)$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f(x + y) = f(x) \cdot f(y)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$ with $\frac{x}{y} \in \left(10^6 - 10^{-6}, 10^6 + 10^{-6}\right)$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$ where $\frac{x}{y} < 10^6 - 10^{-6}$ or $\frac{x}{y} > 10^6 + 10^{-6}$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) + xy
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\frac{x}{y} \in \left(10^6 - 10^{-6}, 10^6 + 10^{-6}\right)$.

positive_text: Find the minimum and maximum values of $S = \frac{p}{q} + \frac{r}{s}$, where $p, q, r, s \in \mathbb{N}$ with $p + r = 20202$ and $q + s = 20200$.

negatives.text: Find the minimum and maximum of $S = \frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d}$ where $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $a + c = 20202$, $b + d = 20200$, and $a, b, c, d$ are all even numbers.
Find the minimum and maximum of $S = \frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d}$ where $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $a + c = 20202$, $b + d = 20200$, and $a > c$.

positive_text: In a round-robin football tournament with $n \ge 4$ teams, each team plays every other team exactly once. The final points tally for the teams are $n$ consecutive integers. What is the largest possible score that the top team can achieve?

negatives.text: In a football tournament between $n \ge 4$ teams, each pair of teams play against each other exactly once. In the final scoreboard, the scores of the teams for the tournament are $n$ consecutive even numbers. Find the maximum possible value for the score of the tournament winning team.

In a football tournament between $n \ge 4$ teams, each pair of teams play against each other exactly once. In the final scoreboard, the scores of the teams for the tournament are $n$ consecutive integers, but the point system is different: a team gets 2 points for a win, 1 for a tie, and 0 for a loss. Find the maximum possible value for the score of the tournament winning team.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer greater than 2. Define $n$ to be $k$-beta if there exist distinct elements $a$ and $b$ in $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}$ such that $ab = k\left(\sum_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq n \\ i \neq a,b}} i\right)$. Determine all $k$-beta integers for each positive integer $k$.

negatives.text: An integer number $n > 2$ is called $k$-beta if two different numbers can be chosen from the set $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}$ so that their product is equal to $k$ times the sum of all $n$ numbers. For each positive integer $k$, find all the $k$-beta numbers.

An integer number $n > 2$ is called $k$-beta if two different numbers can be chosen from the set $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}$ so that their sum is equal to $k$ times the product of the other $n-2$ numbers. For each positive integer $k$, find all the $k$-beta numbers.

An integer number $n > 2$ is called $k$-beta if two different numbers can be chosen from the set $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}$ so that their product is equal to $k$ times the sum of the other $n-2$ numbers, and the two numbers are both even. For each positive integer $k$, find all the $k$-beta numbers.

positive_text: Let $b \ge 2$ and $m \ge 3$ be integers. Prove that there exists an index $i$ such that $b^{m+i-1} + 1$ is relatively prime to all other $b^{m+j-1} + 1$ for $j \ne i$, in the range $1 \le i, j \le n - 1$, when considering the sequence $b^m + 1, b^{m+1} + 1, \dots, b^{2m-2} + 1$.

negatives.text:
Let $a \ge 2$ and $n \ge 3$ be integers. Show that one of the numbers
$$
a^n - 1, a^{n+1} - 1, \dots, a^{2n-2} - 1,
$$
does not share any odd divisor greater than 1 with any other number in the set.

Let $a \ge 2$ and $n \ge 3$ be integers. Show that one of the numbers
$$
a^n + 1, a^{n+1} + 1, \dots, a^{2n-1} + 1,
$$
does not share any odd divisor greater than 1 with any other number in the set.

Let $a \ge 2$ and $n \ge 3$ be integers. Show that one of the numbers
$$
a^n + 1, a^{n+1} + 1, \dots, a^{2n-2} + 1,
$$
has no common divisor (not necessarily odd) greater than 1 with any other number in the set.

positive_text: Consider a solitaire game where a player begins with a positive integer $n$. At each step, the player selects a positive odd divisor $d$ of the current number. If $d = 1$, the number is incremented by 1. Otherwise, the number is divided by $d$. The game proceeds iteratively. For example: $$ 20 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 21 \xrightarrow{\{d=3\}} 7 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 8 \xrightarrow{\{\dots\}} $$ Is there a starting number $n$ for which the sequence of numbers generated in this game never includes any power of 3?

negatives.text: Alan plays a solitaire game in his computer. To begin, Alan chooses a positive integer $n$. Then he chooses a positive odd divisor of $n$. If the chosen divisor is $d=1$, the computer replaces $n$ with $n-1$. If the chosen divisor is a number $d$ greater than 1, the computer replaces $n$ with $n/d$. Alan continues the game by choosing a divisor $d$ of the new number. Can Alan choose an appropriate starting number $n$ and play in such a way that the computer never shows a power of 3?

Alan plays a solitaire game in his computer. To begin, Alan chooses a positive integer $n$. Then he chooses a positive odd divisor of $n$. If the chosen divisor is $d=1$, the computer replaces $n$ with $n+1$. If the chosen divisor is a number $d$ greater than 1, the computer replaces $n$ with $n^2/d$. Alan continues the game by choosing a divisor $d$ of the new number. Can Alan choose an appropriate starting number $n$ and play in such a way that the computer never shows a power of 3?

Alan plays a solitaire game in his computer. To begin, Alan chooses a positive integer $n$. Then he chooses a positive odd divisor of $n$. If the chosen divisor is $d=1$, the computer replaces $n$ with $n+1$. If the chosen divisor is a number $d$ greater than 1, the computer replaces $n$ with $n/d$. Alan continues the game by choosing a divisor $d$ of the new number. Can Alan choose an appropriate starting number $n$ and play in such a way that the computer never shows a power of 2?

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle A = \angle C$ and the internal angle bisector of $\angle B$ passing through the midpoint of $CD$. If $CD = 3AD$, determine $\frac{AB}{BC}$.

negatives.text: In convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the angles at $A$ and $C$ are equal and the bisector of $\angle B$ passes through the midpoint of side $AD$. Given that $CD = 3AD$, find the ratio $\frac{AB}{BC}$.
In convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the angles at $A$ and $C$ are equal and the bisector of $\angle B$ passes through the midpoint of side $CD$. Given that $CD = 2AD$, find the ratio $\frac{AB}{BC}$.
In convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the angles at $A$ and $C$ are equal and the bisector of $\angle B$ passes through the midpoint of side $CD$. Given that $CD = 3AD$, find the ratio $\frac{AB}{BD}$.

positive_text: Let an $n \times n$ grid be colored with two colors, black and white. A coloring is defined as *nice* if all $2 \times 2$ subgrids have an even number of black cells and every cross shape (one cell vertically and one horizontally centered on a cell) has an odd number of black cells. Determine all $n \ge 3$ for which the corners of the grid must all be the same color in every nice coloring.

negatives.text: Each cell of an $n \times n$ grid square is colored black or white. A coloring is *nice* if every $2 \times 2$ square covers an odd number of black cells, and every cross covers an odd number of black cells. Find all $n \ge 3$ such that in each nice coloring the four corner cells have the same color.

Each cell of an $n \times n$ grid square is colored black or white. A coloring is *nice* if every $2 \times 2$ square covers an even number of black cells, and every cross covers an even number of black cells. Find all $n \ge 3$ such that in each nice coloring the four corner cells have the same color.

Each cell of an $n \times n$ grid square is colored black or white. A coloring is *nice* if every $2 \times 2$ square covers an even number of black cells, and every cross covers an odd number of black cells. Find all $n \ge 3$ such that in each nice coloring the four corner cells have different colors.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle with $AB = 3$ and $BC = 2$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AB$ such that the angle bisector of $\angle CDP$ intersects the midpoint of $BC$. Determine the length $BP$.

negatives.text: Rectangle $ABCD$ has sides $AB = 3$, $BC = 2$. Point $P$ on side $AB$ is such that the bisector of $\angle CDB$ passes through the midpoint of $BC$. Find $BP$.
Rectangle $ABCD$ has sides $AB = 3$, $BC = 2$. Point $P$ on side $AB$ is such that the bisector of $\angle DCP$ passes through the midpoint of $BC$. Find $BP$.
Rectangle $ABCD$ has sides $AB = 3$, $BC = 2$. Point $P$ on side $AB$ is such that the bisector of $\angle CDP$ passes through the midpoint of $AD$. Find $BP$.

positive_text: Let $x$ and $y$ be rational numbers such that $x^2 + y^2 = x + y$. If the shared value $t = x + y = x^2 + y^2$ is not an integer, and is expressed in lowest terms as $t = \frac{p}{q}$, let $r$ be the smallest prime factor of $q$. Determine the minimum possible value of $r$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be rational numbers such that $a + b = a^2 - b^2$. Suppose that the common value $s = a + b = a^2 - b^2$ is not an integer, and write it as an irreducible fraction: $s = \frac{m}{n}$. Let $p$ be the least prime divisor of $n$. Find the minimum value of $p$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be rational numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 < a + b$. Suppose that the value $s = a + b$ is not an integer and can be written as an irreducible fraction $s = \frac{m}{n}$. Let $p$ be the least prime divisor of $n$. Find the minimum value of $p$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be rational numbers such that $a + b = a^2 + b^2$. Suppose that the common value $s = a + b = a^2 + b^2$ is not an integer, and write it as an irreducible fraction: $s = \frac{m}{n}$. Let $p$ be the largest prime divisor of $n$. Find the minimum value of $p$.

positive_text: Let $\Gamma$ be a circle and $P$ a point outside of it. Let $PA$ be a tangent from $P$ to $\Gamma$. A line $l$ through $P$ intersects $\Gamma$ at $B$ and $C$, with $B$ between $P$ and $C$. Let $D$ be the reflection of $B$ over $P$. Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be the circumcircles of $\triangle DAC$ and $\triangle PAB$, respectively. Let $E$ be the second intersection of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. The line $EB$ meets $\omega_1$ again at $F$. Prove that $CF = AB$.

negatives.text: Let $\Gamma$ be a circle and $P$ a point outside of it. Let $PA$ be a tangent from $P$ to $\Gamma$. A line $l$ through $P$ intersects $\Gamma$ at $B$ and $C$, with $B$ between $P$ and $C$. Let $D$ be the reflection of $B$ over $P$. Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be the circumcircles of $\triangle DAC$ and $\triangle PAB$, respectively. Let $E$ be the second intersection of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. The line $EB$ meets $\omega_1$ again at $F$. Prove that $CF = 2AB$.

Let $\Gamma$ be a circle and $P$ a point outside of it. Let $PA$ be a tangent from $P$ to $\Gamma$. A line $l$ through $P$ intersects $\Gamma$ at $B$ and $C$, with $B$ between $P$ and $C$. Let $D$ be the reflection of $B$ over $P$. Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be the circumcircles of $\triangle DAC$ and $\triangle PAB$, respectively. Let $E$ be the second intersection of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. The line $EB$ meets $\omega_1$ again at $F$. Prove that $CF = AB^2$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Let $E$ and $F$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AE = AF$. Let $P \ne A$ be the second point of intersection of the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ with $\Gamma$. Let $G$ and $H$ be the other points of intersection of lines $PE$ and $PF$ with $\Gamma$. Let $J$ and $K$ be the intersections of lines $DG$ and $DH$ with $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Prove that the line $JK$ passes through the midpoint of $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and $D$ the midpoint of the smaller arc $BC$ of $\Gamma$. Let $E$ and $F$ be points on the segments $AB$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AE = 2AF$. Let $P \ne A$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ with $\Gamma$. Let $G$ and $H$ be the points, different from $P$, where the lines $PE$ and $PF$ intersect $\Gamma$, respectively. Let $J$ and $K$ be the intersections of the lines $DG$ and $DH$ with the lines $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Prove that the line $JK$ passes through the midpoint of $BC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and $D$ the midpoint of the smaller arc $BC$ of $\Gamma$. Let $E$ and $F$ be points on the segments $AB$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AE = AF$. Let $P \ne A$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ with $\Gamma$. Let $G$ and $H$ be the points, different from $P$, where the lines $PE$ and $PF$ intersect $\Gamma$, respectively. Let $J$ and $K$ be the intersections of the lines $DG$ and $DH$ with the lines $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Prove that the line $JK$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and $D$ the midpoint of the larger arc $BC$ of $\Gamma$. Let $E$ and $F$ be points on the segments $AB$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AE = AF$. Let $P \ne A$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ with $\Gamma$. Let $G$ and $H$ be the points, different from $P$, where the lines $PE$ and $PF$ intersect $\Gamma$, respectively. Let $J$ and $K$ be the intersections of the lines $DG$ and $DH$ with the lines $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Prove that the line $JK$ passes through the midpoint of $BC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram. Construct a square $BDXY$ outside triangle $ABD$ and a square $ACZW$ outside triangle $ADC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the centers of squares $BDXY$ and $ACZW$, respectively. Prove that the distance from $A$ to $P$ equals the distance from $D$ to $Q$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram. Construct a square $BDXY$ with no interior points in common with the triangle $ABD$ and a square $ACZW$ with no interior points in common with the triangle $ADC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the centers of the squares $BDXY$ and $ACZW$ respectively. Prove that $AP > DQ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram. Construct a square $BDXY$ with no interior points in common with the triangle $ABD$ and a square $ACZW$ with no interior points in common with the triangle $ABC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the centers of the squares $BDXY$ and $ACZW$ respectively. Prove that $AP = DQ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram. Construct a square $BDXY$ with no interior points in common with the triangle $ABD$ and a square $ACZW$ with no interior points in common with the triangle $ADC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the centers of the squares $BDXY$ and $ACZW$ respectively. Prove that $AP = CQ$.

positive_text: Sea $A$ un conjunto de enteros positivos distintos. Llamamos a $A$ \emph{\textit{singular}} si, al remover cualquier elemento $a \in A$, los elementos restantes pueden dividirse en dos subconjuntos disjuntos con igual suma. Determine el menor entero $n > 1$ para el cual existe un conjunto $A$ con $n$ elementos que sea singular.

negatives.text: Un conjunto de enteros positivos distintos se llama \emph{\textit{singular}} si, al tachar cualquier elemento, los restantes se pueden agrupar en dos conjuntos con igual \textit{producto}. Hallar el menor entero $n > 1$ tal que existe un conjunto singular con $n$ elementos.

Un conjunto de enteros positivos distintos se llama \emph{\textit{singular}} si, al tachar cualquier elemento, los restantes se pueden agrupar en dos conjuntos con igual suma, pero uno de los conjuntos debe contener al menos dos elementos. Hallar el menor entero $n > 1$ tal que existe un conjunto singular con $n$ elementos.

Un conjunto de enteros positivos distintos se llama \emph{\textit{singular}} si, al tachar cualquier elemento, los restantes se pueden agrupar en dos conjuntos con igual suma, y el conjunto debe contener números impares. Hallar el menor entero $n > 1$ tal que existe un conjunto singular con $n$ elementos.

positive_text: Dado un entero $k > 1$, hallar el menor entero positivo $n$ tal que existe una configuración de $k$ casillas negras en cada fila y en cada columna de un tablero $n \times n$, de forma que cada casilla negra esté aislada de las demás, es decir, no comparta ni lado ni vértice con otra casilla negra.

negatives.text: Sea $k > 1$ un entero. Determinar el menor entero positivo $n$ tal que algunas casillas de un tablero de $n \times n$ se pueden pintar de negro de modo que en cada fila y en cada columna haya exactamente $k$ casillas negras, y además, las casillas negras no compartan un lado con otra casilla negra.

Sea $k > 1$ un entero. Determinar el menor entero positivo $n$ tal que algunas casillas de un tablero de $n \times n$ se pueden pintar de negro de modo que en cada fila y en cada columna haya exactamente $k$ casillas negras, y además, las casillas negras no compartan ni un lado ni un vértice con una casilla blanca.

Sea $k > 1$ un entero. Determinar el menor entero positivo $n$ tal que algunas casillas de un tablero de $n \times n$ se pueden pintar de negro de modo que en cada fila y en cada columna haya exactamente $k$ casillas negras, y además, las casillas negras no compartan ni un lado ni un vértice con otra casilla negra, excepto en una fila.

positive_text:
Sea $n \ge 3$ un entero. En un polígono regular de $n$ lados, un vértice ha sido designado como *trampa*. Matías coloca una ficha en algún vértice y, en cada turno, Lucas elige un entero positivo. Matías entonces mueve la ficha ese número de vértices, en sentido horario o antihorario, a su elección.

a) Hallar todos los $n \ge 3$ para los cuales Matías puede garantizar que la ficha nunca caiga en la trampa, sin importar las elecciones de Lucas. Describir una estrategia.

b) Hallar todos los $n \ge 3$ para los cuales Lucas puede asegurar que Matías termine en la trampa. Describir una estrategia para Lucas.

negatives.text:
Sea $n \ge 3$ un entero. Lucas y Matías juegan en un polígono regular de $n$ lados, con dos vértices marcados como *trampas*. Matías coloca una ficha en un vértice y, en cada paso, Lucas elige un entero positivo. Matías mueve la ficha ese número de vértices en sentido horario o antihorario, a su elección.

a) Determinar todos los $n \ge 3$ tales que Matías puede garantizar que la ficha nunca caiga en ninguna trampa, sin importar las elecciones de Lucas.

b) Determinar todos los $n \ge 3$ tales que Lucas puede forzar a Matías a caer en al menos una trampa.

Sea $n \ge 3$ un entero. Lucas y Matías juegan en un polígono regular de $n$ lados, con un vértice marcado como *trampa*. Matías coloca una ficha en un vértice y, en cada paso, Lucas elige un entero positivo. Matías debe mover la ficha ese número de vértices, pero únicamente en sentido horario.

a) Determinar todos los $n \ge 3$ tales que Matías puede evitar caer en la trampa, independientemente de las elecciones de Lucas.

b) Determinar todos los $n \ge 3$ tales que Lucas puede forzar a Matías a caer en la trampa.

positive_text: Determinar todos los enteros $n > 1$ para los cuales existe una disposición sin repeticiones de los números $1$ a $n^2$ en un tablero de $n \times n$ tal que la media aritmética de los números en cada fila y cada columna es un entero.

negatives.text: Hallar todos los enteros $n > 1$ para los que es posible escribir en las casillas de un tablero de $n \times n$ los números enteros desde $1$ hasta $n^2$, sin repeticiones, de modo que en cada fila y en cada columna el promedio de los $n$ números escritos sea un número par.

Determinar todos los enteros $n > 1$ para los cuales existe una disposición sin repeticiones de los números $1$ a $n^2$ en un tablero de $n \times n$ tal que el promedio de los números en cada fila sea un entero, pero no se requiere lo mismo para las columnas.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB < AC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on the internal bisector of $\angle BAC$, with $X$ closer to $A$ than $Y$, and such that $BX \parallel CY$. Let $Z$ be the reflection of $X$ across line $BC$. Let $P$ be the intersection of $YZ$ and $BC$. If $K = BY \cap CX$, show that $KA = KP$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. On the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, two points $X$ and $Y$ are marked such that $X$ is between $A$ and $Y$, and $BX$ is perpendicular to $CY$. Let $Z$ be the reflection of $X$ with respect to $BC$. Let $P$ be the point of intersection of lines $YZ$ and $BC$. If lines $BY$ and $CX$ intersect at $K$, prove that $KA = KP$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. On the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, two points $X$ and $Y$ are marked such that $X$ is between $A$ and $Y$, and $BX$ is parallel to $CY$. Let $Z$ be the reflection of $Y$ with respect to $BC$. Let $P$ be the point of intersection of lines $YZ$ and $BC$. If lines $BY$ and $CX$ intersect at $K$, prove that $KA = KP$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. On the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, two points $X$ and $Y$ are marked such that $X$ is between $A$ and $Y$, and $BX$ is parallel to $CY$. Let $Z$ be the reflection of $X$ with respect to $BC$. Let $P$ be the point of intersection of lines $YZ$ and $BC$. If lines $AY$ and $CX$ intersect at $K$, prove that $KA = KP$.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. The incircle of $ABC$ touches side $BC$ at point $D$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the rays $IB$ and $IC$ respectively, with the property that $\angle IAP = \angle CAD$ and $\angle IAQ = \angle BAD$. Show that the lengths $AP$ and $AQ$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. The incircle of $ABC$ is tangent to side $BC$ at $D$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points on rays $IB$ and $IC$ respectively such that $\angle IAP = 2\angle CAD$ and $\angle IAQ = 2\angle BAD$. Prove that $AP = AQ$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = CD$, $\angle BCD = 2\angle BAD$, $\angle ABC = 2\angle ADC$, and $\angle BAD \neq \angle ADC$. Determine the angle formed by the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB = CD$, $\angle BCD = 2\angle BAD$, $\angle ABC = 2\angle ADC$, and $\angle BAD = \angle ADC$. Find the angle between diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = CD$, $\angle BCD = 2\angle BAD$, $\angle ABC = 3\angle ADC$, and $\angle BAD \neq \angle ADC$. Find the angle between diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB = CD$, $\angle BCD = 2\angle BAD$, $\angle ABC = 2\angle ADC$, and $\angle BAD \neq \angle ADC$. Find the length of diagonal $AC$.

positive_text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers. For each positive integer $m$, define
$$
T_m = a_1^m + a_2^m + \dots + a_n^m.
$$
(a) Prove that if $T_1 < T_2$ the sequence $T_1, T_2, T_3, \dots$ is strictly increasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible that $T_1 > T_2$ and yet the sequence $T_1, T_2, T_3, \dots$ is not strictly decreasing.

negatives.text:
Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive real numbers. For each positive integer $k$, define
$$
S_k = x_1^k + x_2^k + \dots + x_n^k.
$$
(a) Prove that if $S_1 < S_2$ the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible that $S_1 > S_2$ and yet the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is not strictly increasing.

Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive real numbers. For each positive integer $k$, define
$$
S_k = x_1^k + x_2^k + \dots + x_n^k.
$$
(a) Prove that if $S_1 < S_2$ the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is non-decreasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible that $S_1 > S_2$ and yet the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is not non-increasing.

Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive real numbers. For each positive integer $k$, define
$$
S_k = x_1^{-k} + x_2^{-k} + \dots + x_n^{-k}.
$$
(a) Prove that if $S_1 < S_2$ the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is strictly increasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible that $S_1 > S_2$ and yet the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is not strictly decreasing.

positive_text:
Show that the equation
$$
6(6x^2 + 3y^2 + z^2) = 5w^2
$$
has no integer solutions other than $x = y = z = w = 0$.

negatives.text:
Prove that the equation
$$
6(6a^2 - 3b^2 + c^2) = 5n^2
$$
has no solutions in integers except $a = b = c = n = 0$.

Prove that the equation
$$
6(6a^2 + 3b^2 + c^2) = 5n^3
$$
has no solutions in integers except $a = b = c = n = 0$.

positive_text: Let $P_{1}$, $P_{2}$, $P_{3}$ be three points in the plane, and define $P_{4}=P_{1}$, $P_{5}=P_{2}$. For $n=1,2,3$, let $M_{n}$ be the midpoint of $P_{n}P_{n+1}$, and let $N_{n}$ be the midpoint of $P_{n}M_{n}$. Suppose that $P_{n}N_{n+1}$ and $M_{n}P_{n+2}$ intersect at $X_{n}$, and that $P_{n}M_{n+1}$ and $N_{n}P_{n+2}$ intersect at $Y_{n}$. Compute the ratio of the area of triangle $X_{1}X_{2}X_{3}$ to the area of triangle $Y_{1}Y_{2}Y_{3}$.

negatives.text: Let $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, $A_{3}$ be three points in the plane, and for convenience, let $A_{4}=A_{1}$, $A_{5}=A_{2}$. For $n=1,2$, and $3$, suppose that $B_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} A_{n+1}$, and suppose that $C_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} B_{n}$. Suppose that $A_{n} C_{n+1}$ and $B_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $D_{n}$, and that $A_{n} B_{n+1}$ and $C_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $E_{n}$. Calculate the ratio of the area of triangle $D_{1} D_{2} D_{3}$ to the area of triangle $E_{1} E_{2} E_{1}$.

Let $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, $A_{3}$ be three points in the plane, and for convenience, let $A_{4}=A_{1}$, $A_{5}=A_{2}$. For $n=1,2$, and $3$, suppose that $B_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} A_{n+1}$, and suppose that $C_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n+1} B_{n}$. Suppose that $A_{n} C_{n+1}$ and $B_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $D_{n}$, and that $A_{n} B_{n+1}$ and $C_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $E_{n}$. Calculate the ratio of the area of triangle $D_{1} D_{2} D_{3}$ to the area of triangle $E_{1} E_{2} E_{3}$.

Let $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, $A_{3}$ be three points in the plane, and for convenience, let $A_{4}=A_{1}$, $A_{5}=A_{2}$. For $n=1,2$, and $3$, suppose that $B_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} A_{n+1}$, and suppose that $C_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} B_{n}$. Suppose that $A_{n} C_{n+1}$ and $B_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $D_{n}$, and that $A_{n+2} B_{n+1}$ and $C_{n} A_{n}$ meet at $E_{n}$. Calculate the ratio of the area of triangle $D_{1} D_{2} D_{3}$ to the area of triangle $E_{1} E_{2} E_{3}$.

positive_text: Prove that for any integer $n \geq 6$, there is a convex hexagon that can be partitioned into precisely $n$ triangles, all of which are congruent to one another.

negatives.text: Show that for every integer $n \geq 6$, there exists a convex hexagon which can be dissected into exactly $n$ congruent quadrilaterals.
Show that for every integer $n \geq 6$, there exists a convex hexagon which can be dissected into exactly $n$ congruent triangles and one central square.
Show that for every integer $n \geq 6$, there exists a convex polygon with six sides that can be dissected into exactly $n$ congruent triangles, all with equal area but not necessarily congruent.

positive_text:
Let $k$ be an integer such that $k > 3$. Suppose that we choose three numbers from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$. Using each of these three numbers only once and using addition, multiplication, and parentheses, we form all possible expressions.

a. Prove that if all three numbers are strictly greater than $k / 2$, then all these expressions evaluate to unique values.

b. Let $q$ be a prime number such that $q \leq \sqrt{k}$. Show that the number of such triplets where the smallest is $q$ and not all expressions yield distinct values is equal to the number of positive divisors of $q-1$.

negatives.text:
Let $n$ be an integer such that $n > 3$. Suppose that we choose three numbers from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. Using each of these three numbers only once and using addition, multiplication, and parenthesis, let us form all possible combinations.

a. Show that if we choose all three numbers greater than or equal to $n / 2$, then the values of these combinations are all distinct.

b. Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p \leq \sqrt{n}$. Show that the number of ways of choosing three numbers so that the smallest one is $p$ and the values of the combinations are not all distinct is precisely the number of positive divisors of $p$.

Let $n$ be an integer such that $n > 3$. Suppose that we choose three numbers from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. Using each of these three numbers only once and using addition, multiplication, and parenthesis, let us form all possible combinations.

a. Show that if we choose all three numbers greater than $n / 2$, then the values of these combinations are all equal.

b. Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p \leq \sqrt{n}$. Show that the number of ways of choosing three numbers so that the smallest one is $p$ and the values of the combinations are not all distinct is equal to the number of positive divisors of $p$.

Let $n$ be an integer such that $n > 3$. Suppose that we choose three numbers from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. Using each of these three numbers only once and using addition, multiplication, and parenthesis, let us form all possible combinations.

a. Show that if we choose all three numbers less than $n / 2$, then the values of these combinations are all distinct.

b. Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p \leq \sqrt{n}$. Show that the number of ways of choosing three numbers so that the smallest one is $p$ and the values of the combinations are not all distinct is equal to the number of positive divisors of $p+1$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with all sides of equal length and $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$. A line $\ell$ passes through $D$ and does not otherwise intersect $ABCD$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the intersections of $\ell$ with $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. If $M$ is the intersection of $CE$ and $AF$, prove that $CA^2 = CM \cdot CE$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with all sides of equal length and $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$. Let $\ell$ be a line through $D$ not intersecting the quadrilateral except at $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the intersections of $\ell$ with $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $M$ be the intersection of $CE$ and $AF$. Prove that $CA^2 = CM \cdot CE$.

positive_text: In an $n \times n$ grid of buildings, each building is identified by a pair $(x, y)$ with $1 \leq x, y \leq n$. At time $t = 0$, a fire starts at the building $(1, c)$, where $c \leq \frac{n}{2}$. In each time step, firefighters can protect one unburned building, while the fire spreads to all unprotected adjacent buildings. Adjacency is defined as Manhattan distance of $1$. The fire continues to spread until no new buildings can be reached. What is the maximum number of buildings that can be saved from the fire?

negatives.text: In an $n \times n$ grid of houses indexed by $(i, j)$, a fire starts at $(1, c)$, where $c \leq \frac{n}{2}$. During each time step, firefighters can defend one house, and the fire spreads to all undefended neighbors of each burning house. However, now the fire spreads to diagonal neighbors as well (i.e., if $|i-k| + |j-\ell| \leq 2$). At most how many houses can be saved?

In an $n \times n$ grid of houses indexed by $(i, j)$, a fire starts at $(1, c)$, where $c \leq \frac{n}{2}$. During each time step, the fire spreads to all undefended neighbors of each burning house, but now firefighters can defend two houses per time step instead of one. At most how many houses can be saved?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Define points $X$ and $Y$ on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $AX = BX + CB - CA$ and $AY = CY + BC - BA$. Let $P$ be a point such that $PX \perp AB$ and $PY \perp AC$. Prove that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A > 60^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $CA + AX = CB + BX$ and $BA + AY = BC + CY$. Let $P$ be the point in the plane such that the lines $PX$ and $PY$ are perpendicular to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $CA + AX = CB - BX$ and $BA + AY = BC - CY$. Let $P$ be the point in the plane such that the lines $PX$ and $PY$ are perpendicular to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $CA + AX = CB + BX$ and $BA + AY = BC + CY$. Let $P$ be the point in the plane such that the lines $PX$ and $PY$ are perpendicular to $BC$ and $AB$, respectively. Prove that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.

positive_text: Given three disjoint circles $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}$ in the plane, and a point $P$ outside all of them, construct for each circle $\omega_{i}$, two distinct points $X_{i}, Y_{i}$ on $\omega_{i}$ such that $PX_{i}$ and $PY_{i}$ are tangent to $\omega_{i}$. Define $P$ to be special if the three lines $X_{1}Y_{1}, X_{2}Y_{2}, X_{3}Y_{3}$ intersect at a single point. Prove that all such special points lie on a common circle.

negatives.text: Given three disjoint circles $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}$ in the plane, and a point $P$ outside all of them, construct for each circle $\omega_{i}$, two distinct points $X_{i}, Y_{i}$ on $\omega_{i}$ such that $PX_{i}$ and $PY_{i}$ are secants to $\omega_{i}$. Define $P$ to be special if the three lines $X_{1}Y_{1}, X_{2}Y_{2}, X_{3}Y_{3}$ intersect at a single point. Prove that all such special points lie on a common circle.

Given three disjoint circles $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}$ in the plane, and a point $P$ outside all of them, construct for each circle $\omega_{i}$, two distinct points $X_{i}, Y_{i}$ on $\omega_{i}$ such that $PX_{i}$ and $PY_{i}$ are tangent to $\omega_{i}$. Define $P$ to be special if the three lines $P X_{1}, P Y_{1}, P X_{2}, P Y_{2}, P X_{3}, P Y_{3}$ intersect at a single point. Prove that all such special points lie on a common circle.

Given three disjoint circles $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}$ in the plane, and a point $P$ outside all of them, construct for each circle $\omega_{i}$, two distinct points $X_{i}, Y_{i}$ on $\omega_{i}$ such that $PX_{i}$ and $PY_{i}$ are tangent to $\omega_{i}$. Define $P$ to be special if the three lines $X_{1}Y_{1}, X_{2}Y_{2}, X_{3}Y_{3}$ are parallel. Prove that all such special points lie on a common circle.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects segment $AB$ at $X$ and the extension of $AC$ beyond $C$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $BXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z \neq B$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZY$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AB = VW$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects side $AB$ at $X$ and ray $AC$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $AXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z \neq A$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZY$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AB = VW$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects side $AB$ at $X$ and ray $AC$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $BXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z \neq B$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZX$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AB = VW$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects side $AB$ at $X$ and ray $AC$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $BXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z \neq B$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZY$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AC = VW$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be called special if, for every point $D$ on segment $BC$, the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and $AC$ are $P$ and $Q$, and the reflection of $D$ across the line $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Show that triangle $ABC$ is special if and only if $\angle A = 90^\circ$ and $AB = AC$.

negatives.text: We say that a triangle $ABC$ is great if the following holds: for any point $D$ on the side $BC$, if $P$ and $Q$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to the lines $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, then the reflection of $D$ in the line $PQ$ lies on the line $BC$. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is great if and only if $\angle A = 90^\circ$ and $AB = AC$.

We say that a triangle $ABC$ is great if the following holds: for any point $D$ on the side $BC$, if $P$ and $Q$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to the lines $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, then the reflection of $D$ in the line $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is great if and only if $\angle A = 60^\circ$ and $AB = AC$.

We say that a triangle $ABC$ is great if the following holds: for any point $D$ on the side $BC$, if $P$ and $Q$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to the lines $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, then the reflection of $D$ in the line $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is great if and only if $\angle A = 90^\circ$ and $AB = 2AC$.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $ f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+} $ satisfying
$$
(a+1) f(b + c) = f(b f(a) + c) + f(c f(a) + b)
$$
for all $ a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^{+} $.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+} $ such that
$$
(z+1) f(x+y) = f(x f(z) + y) - f(y f(z) + x)
$$
for all $ x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{+} $.

Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+} $ such that
$$
(z^2 + 1) f(x+y) = f(x f(z) + y) + f(y f(z) + x)
$$
for all $ x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{+} $.

Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+} $ such that
$$
(z+1) f(x^2 + y^2) = f(x f(z) + y) + f(y f(z) + x)
$$
for all $ x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{+} $.

positive_text: Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Determine all polynomials $Q(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for every infinite sequence $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots$ of integers where each integer in $\mathbb{Z}$ appears exactly once, there exist indices $i<j$ and an integer $m$ satisfying $b_{i} + b_{i+1} + \cdots + b_{j} = Q(m)$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for any infinite sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of integers where each integer in $\mathbb{Z}$ appears exactly once, there exist indices $i<j$ and an integer $k$ such that $a_{i} + a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_{j} = -P(k)$.

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for any infinite sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of integers where each integer in $\mathbb{Z}$ appears exactly once, there exist indices $i<j$ and an integer $k$ such that $a_{i} + a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_{j} = P(k)^2$.

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for any infinite sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of integers where each integer in $\mathbb{Z}$ appears exactly once, there exist indices $i<j$ and an integer $k$ such that $a_{i} + a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_{j} = P(k) + 1$.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 5$ be an integer. Suppose you have $n$ axis-aligned squares with side lengths $1,2, \ldots, n$. These squares can only intersect at their corners, not along edges or interiors. Prove that there exists an arrangement of these squares where each square is adjacent to precisely two others.

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 5$ be an integer. Consider $n$ squares with side lengths $1,2, \ldots, n$. The squares are placed in the plane with sides parallel to the axes. No two squares overlap or share a side, but they may touch at vertices. Prove that it is possible to arrange these squares so that each square touches at least two others.

Let $n \geq 5$ be an integer. Consider $n$ squares with side lengths $1,2, \ldots, n$. These squares are placed in the plane with sides parallel to the axes and are allowed to touch at corners only. Prove that it is possible to arrange these squares so that each square touches exactly one other square.

Let $n \geq 5$ be an integer. Consider $n$ squares with side lengths $1,2, \ldots, n$. The squares are placed in the plane with sides parallel to the axes and may not touch at all. Prove that it is possible to arrange these squares in such a way that each square touches exactly two other squares.

positive_text: Let $\gamma$ and $\delta$ be positive real numbers. A traveler begins at $(0,0)$ and moves each minute either one unit right or one unit up, always staying within the region $|x - y| < 2025$. Upon reaching a point $(x, y)$, she writes the integer $\lfloor x \gamma + y \delta\rfloor$ on it. It is known that every non-negative integer is written exactly once. Determine all such pairs $(\gamma, \delta)$ for which this is possible.

negatives.text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. A traveler moves from $(0,0)$ each minute either one unit right or one unit up, staying within the region $|x - y| < 2025$. Upon reaching a point $(x, y)$, she writes the integer $\lfloor x \alpha - y \beta\rfloor$ on it. It is known that every non-negative integer is written exactly once. Determine all such pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which this is possible.

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. A traveler moves from $(0,0)$ each minute either one unit right or one unit up, staying within the region $|x - y| < 2025$. Upon reaching a point $(x, y)$, she writes the integer $\lfloor x \alpha + y^2 \beta\rfloor$ on it. It is known that every non-negative integer is written exactly once. Determine all such pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which this is possible.

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. A traveler moves from $(0,0)$ each minute either one unit right or one unit up, staying within the region $|x - y| < 2025$. Upon reaching a point $(x, y)$, she writes the integer $\lfloor x \alpha + y \beta\rfloor$ on it. It is known that each integer from $1$ to $100$ is written exactly once. Determine all such pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which this is possible.

positive_text: \text{Show that the expression} \quad \frac{(a-b)^7 + (b-c)^7 + (c-a)^7 - (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)((a-b)^4 + (b-c)^4 + (c-a)^4)}{(a-b)^5 + (b-c)^5 + (c-a)^5} \ge 3 \quad \text{is true for all distinct integers } a, b, c. \text{Determine when equality occurs.}

negatives.text: \text{Prove that} \quad \frac{(x-y)^7 + (y-z)^7 + (z-x)^7 + (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)((x-y)^4 + (y-z)^4 + (z-x)^4)}{(x-y)^5 + (y-z)^5 + (z-x)^5} \ge 3 \quad \text{for all distinct integers } x, y, z. \text{When does equality hold?}

\text{Prove that} \quad \frac{(x-y)^7 + (y-z)^7 + (z-x)^7 - (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)((x-y)^3 + (y-z)^3 + (z-x)^3)}{(x-y)^5 + (y-z)^5 + (z-x)^5} \ge 3 \quad \text{for all distinct integers } x, y, z. \text{When does equality hold?}

\text{Prove that} \quad \frac{(x-y)^7 + (y-z)^7 + (z-x)^7 - (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)((x-y)^4 + (y-z)^4 + (z-x)^4)}{(x-y)^4 + (y-z)^4 + (z-x)^4} \ge 3 \quad \text{for all distinct integers } x, y, z. \text{When does equality hold?}

positive_text:
Find all real solutions $(a, b, c)$ such that
$$
4a^4 - a^2(4b^4 + 4c^4 - 1) - 2abc + b^8 + 2b^4c^4 + b^2c^2 + c^8 = 0.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all real solutions $(x, y, z)$ such that
$$
4x^4 - x^2(4y^4 + 4z^4 - 1) + 2xyz + y^8 + 2y^4z^4 + y^2z^2 + z^8 = 0.
$$

Find all real solutions $(x, y, z)$ such that
$$
4x^4 - x^2(4y^4 + 4z^4 - 1) - 2xyz + y^8 + 2y^4z^4 + y^2z^2 + z^8 = 1.
$$

Find all real solutions $(x, y, z)$ such that
$$
4x^4 - x^2(4y^4 + 4z^4 - 1) - 2xyz + y^8 + 2y^4z^4 + y^2z^2 + z^6 = 0.
$$

positive_text: Find all ordered triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers $a > b > c > 0$ satisfying the equation $a^2 = b \cdot 2^a + 1$.

negatives.text: Find all ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers $x > y > z > 0$ such that $x^2 = y \cdot 2^x - 1$ holds.
Determine all triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers $x > y > z > 0$ such that $x^2 = y \cdot 2^y + 1$ holds.

positive_text: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers with $a + b = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{(3a - 1)^2}{a} + \frac{(3b - 1)^2}{b} \geq 1.$$ When does equality hold?

negatives.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers with $x + y = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{(3x - 1)^2}{x} + \frac{(3y - 1)^2}{y} \geq 2.$$ When does equality hold?
Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers with $x + y = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{(3x + 1)^2}{x} + \frac{(3y + 1)^2}{y} \geq 1.$$ When does equality hold?
Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers with $x + y = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{(3x - 1)^2}{x} + \frac{(3y - 1)^2}{y} \leq 1.$$ When does equality hold?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle ABC = \angle BAC$, and let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ on the arc $AC$ that does not include $B$. If $E$ and $F$ are the feet of perpendiculars from $C$ to the lines $AP$ and $BP$, respectively, show that $AE = BF$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$ and $P$ be a point on the circumcircle lying on the arc $CA$ not containing $B$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the feet of perpendiculars from $C$ to the lines $AP$ and $CP$, respectively. Prove that $AE = BF$.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$ and $P$ be a point on the circumcircle lying on the arc $CA$ not containing $B$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the feet of perpendiculars from $C$ to the lines $AP$ and $BP$, respectively. Prove that $AE > BF$.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$, $z$ and $w$ be four integers such that $7x + 8y = 14z + 28w$. Prove that $x \cdot y$ is divisible by $14$.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be four integers such that $7a + 8b = 14c + 28d^2$. Prove that $a \cdot b$ is a multiple of $14$.

positive_text:
A courier has $n$ items of masses $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, $n$. She wants to partition the items into three subsets with the same total mass. Can this be done for

a. $n = 2011$

b. $n = 2012$?

negatives.text:
A postman has $n$ parcels of weights $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, $n$. He wants to divide the parcels into three groups of equal weight. Is this possible for

a. $n = 2011$

b. $n = -2012$?

A postman has $n$ parcels of weights $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, $n$. He wants to divide the parcels into three groups of equal weight. Is this possible for

a. $n = 2011$

b. $n = 2012^2$?

A postman has $n$ parcels of weights $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, $n$. He wants to divide the parcels into three groups of equal weight. Is this possible for

a. $n = 2011$

b. $n = 2012$, but only using even-numbered parcels?

positive_text:
Find all integers $a$ and $b$ satisfying
$$
(a - 1)a + a + 1 + (b - 1)b + b + 1 = 24 - 9ab.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integer solutions of the equation
$$
(x - 1)x + (x + 1) + (y - 1)y + (y + 1) = 24 + 9xy.
$$

Find all integer solutions of the equation
$$
(x - 1)x + (x + 1) + (y - 1)y + (y + 1) = 24 - 9x^2y.
$$

Find all integer solutions of the equation
$$
(x - 1)x + (x + 1) + (y - 1)y + (y + 1) = 24 - 9x(y + 1).
$$

positive_text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. Given a convex polygon $A_1A_2\dots A_n$, consider a line $\ell$ passing through $A_1$ but not containing any other vertex. Let $k$ be the line perpendicular to $\ell$ at $A_1$. The polygon is orthogonally projected onto $k$, yielding points $C_j$ as the images of $A_j$. If the projections $C_j$ are all distinct, the line $\ell$ is called valid. Over all convex $n$-gons and valid lines $\ell$, how many distinct orderings of the points $C_1, \dots, C_n$ can occur?

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. For a convex $n$-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_n$, consider a line $g$ through $A_1$ that does not contain any other vertex. How many different orderings of the points $B_1, \dots, B_n$ exist?

positive_text:

holds for all real numbers $ X $ and $ Y $. For which values of $ X $ and $ Y $ does equality hold for this smallest constant $ C $?

$$
(X + Y)^2 (X^2 + Y^2 + C) + (1 - XY)^2 \leq 0
$$
holds for all real numbers $ X $ and $ Y $. For which values of $ X $ and $ Y $ does equality hold for this smallest constant $ C $?

$$
(X + Y)^2 (X^2 + Y^2 + C^2) + (1 - XY)^2 \geq 0
$$
holds for all real numbers $ X $ and $ Y $. For which values of $ X $ and $ Y $ does equality hold for this smallest constant $ C $?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $AB > AC$. Let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to the opposite sides. Let $S$ be the intersection point of line $EF$ with side $BC$. Show that the circumcircles of triangles $AEF$ and $DES$ are tangent at point $E$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$. Let $D$, $E$ and $F$ denote the feet of its altitudes on $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Let $S$ denote the intersection of lines $EF$ and $BC$. Prove that the circumcircles $k_1$ and $k_2$ of the two triangles $AEF$ and $DFS$ touch in $E$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that $11$ divides $n^5 + 5^n$ if and only if $11$ divides $n^5 \cdot 5^n + 1$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that $n^5 - 5^n$ is divisible by $11$ if and only if $n^5 \cdot 5^n + 1$ is divisible by $11$.
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that $n^5 + 5^n$ is divisible by $11$ if and only if $n^5 \cdot 5^n - 1$ is divisible by $11$.
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that $n^5 + 5^n$ is divisible by $11$ if and only if $n^5 + 5^n \cdot 1$ is divisible by $11$.

positive_text:
Determine all integer triples $(a, b, c)$ such that
$$
3^{a} - 5^{b} = c^{2}
$$

negatives.text:

$$

positive_text: Let $P_0, P_1, \dots, P_5$ be a circular labelling of six distinct points on a circle with centre $O$, and define $Q_i$ to be the midpoint of the segment $P_iP_{i+1}$, $i = 0, 1, \dots, 5$ (indices modulo $6$). Suppose no opposite sides of the hexagon $P_0P_1\cdots P_5$ are parallel. A line through $O$ intersects the circle $Q_iOQ_{i+3}$ at a second point $R_i$, $i = 0, 1, 2$. Let $m_i$ be the tangent to the circle $Q_iOQ_{i+3}$ at $R_i$, $i = 0, 1, 2$. The lines $m_i$ and $m_j$ intersect to define the point $S_k$, where $\{i, j, k\} = \{0, 1, 2\}$. Prove that the circles $Q_iOQ_{i+3}$ and the circle $S_0S_1S_2$ have a common point in the plane.

negatives.text: Let $A_0, A_1, \dots, A_5$ be a circular labelling of six distinct points on a circle centred at $O$, and let $B_i$ be the midpoint of the segment $A_iA_{i+1}$, $i = 0, 1, \dots, 5$ (indices modulo $6$). Assume no opposite sides of the hexagon $A_0A_1\cdots A_5$ are parallel. A line through $O$ meets the circle $B_iOB_{i+3}$ at the point $C_i$, $i = 0, 1, 2$. Let $\ell_i$ be the line joining $O$ and $C_i$, $i = 0, 1, 2$. The lines $\ell_i$ and $\ell_j$ meet to define the point $D_k$, where $\{i, j, k\} = \{0, 1, 2\}$. Prove that the three circles $B_iOB_{i+3}$ and the circle $D_0D_1D_2$ have a common point in the plane.

Let $A_0, A_1, \dots, A_5$ be a circular labelling of six distinct points on a circle centred at $O$, and let $B_i$ be the midpoint of the segment $A_iA_{i+1}$, $i = 0, 1, \dots, 5$ (indices modulo $6$). Assume no opposite sides of the hexagon $A_0A_1\cdots A_5$ are parallel. A line through $O$ meets the circle $B_iOB_{i+3}$ at the point $C_i$, $i = 0, 1, 2$. Let $\ell_i$ be the tangent to the circle $B_iOB_{i+3}$ at the point $C_i$, $i = 0, 1, 2$. The lines $\ell_i$ and $\ell_j$ intersect at a point $D_k$, where $\{i, j, k\} = \{0, 1, 2\}$. Prove that the three circles $B_iOB_{i+3}$ and the line $D_0D_1D_2$ intersect at a common point in the plane.

positive_text:
Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $a, b: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $a(n) = b(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$ where $\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of all integers. Define $c: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
c(n) = \max \{a(k)b(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} c(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (a(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (b(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$ where $\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of all integers. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \min \{f(k)g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$ where $\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of all integers. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \sum \{f(k)g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$ where $\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of all integers. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by

h(n) = \max \{f(k)^2g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

positive_text: Find all positive integer solutions $(a, b, c, d)$ satisfying $$12^a + 13^b - 14^c = 2013^d.$$

negatives.text: Determine all quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ of positive integers, such that $$12^x + 13^y + 14^z = 2013^t.$$
Determine all quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ of positive integers, such that $$12^x + 13^y - 14^z = 2013^t + 1.$$
Determine all quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ of positive integers, such that $$12^x + 13^y - 14^z = 2013^{t+1}.$$

positive_text:
Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $b_1$, $b_2$ and $b_3$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
(a_1 - b_1)(a_2 - b_2)(a_3 - b_3) = a_1 a_2 a_3 - b_1 b_2 b_3.
$$
Prove that
$$
(a_1 + b_1)(a_2 + b_2)(a_3 + b_3) \geq 8a_1 a_2 a_3.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$, $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
(m_1 + n_1)(m_2 + n_2)(m_3 + n_3) = m_1 m_2 m_3 + n_1 n_2 n_3.
$$
Prove that
$$
(m_1 - n_1)(m_2 - n_2)(m_3 - n_3) \geq 8m_1 m_2 m_3.
$$

$$

positive_text: Given isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $H$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $M$ to $AB$. negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and $H$ the projection of $M$ onto $AB$. positive_text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle ($\omega$) with centre $O$. Let $M$ be a point on segment $AB$ such that $MA < MB$, and define circles ($\omega_1$) and ($\omega_2$) with diameters $AM$ and $BM$ respectively. If the common chord of the circumcircles of triangles $CED$ and $CFG$ intersects $\omega$ at points $K$ and $L$, and intersects ($\omega_2$) at point $N$ (with $N$ closer to $L$), prove that $KC = NL$.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle ($\omega$) with centre $O$. positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that } \sqrt{x^3 y + x^3 z} + \sqrt{y^3 z + y^3 x} + \sqrt{z^3 x + z^3 y} \geq \frac{4}{3}(xy + yz + zx)

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that } \sqrt{a^3 b - a^3 c} + \sqrt{b^3 c - b^3 a} + \sqrt{c^3 a - c^3 b} \geq \frac{4}{3}(ab + bc + ca)

positive_text:
Determine all increasing or decreasing functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for any $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ and $ n \in \mathbb{N} $,
$$
\left| \sum_{k=1}^{n} k (f(x + k + 1) - f(f(x + k))) \right| < C
$$
with $ C > 0 $ independent of $ x $ and $ n $.

negatives.text:
Find all monotonic functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for all real $ x $ and natural $ n $,
$$
\left| \sum_{i=1}^{n} i (f(x + i - 1) - f^2(x + i)) \right| < C
$$
where $ C > 0 $ is fixed and $ f^2(x) = f(f(x)) $.

Find all monotonic functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for all real $ x $ and natural $ n $,
$$
\left| \sum_{i=1}^{n} i (f(x + i + 1) - f^2(x + i)) \right| > C
$$
where $ C > 0 $ is fixed and $ f^2(x) = f(f(x)) $.

Find all monotonic functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for all real $ x $ and natural $ n $,
$$
\left| \sum_{i=1}^{n} i (f(x + i + 1)^2 - f^2(x + i)) \right| < C
$$
where $ C > 0 $ is fixed and $ f^2(x) = f(f(x)) $.

positive_text: Suppose triangle $ABC$ satisfies $AB < AC$. On the rays $BA$ and $CA$ we choose points $F$ and $E$ such that $BF = CE = BC$. positive_text: Let $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ be any set of points in the plane. Define $R(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n)$ as the radius of the smallest circle enclosing all these points. Show that when $n \ge 3$, there exist indices $i, j, k$ such that $$ R(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n) = R(P_i, P_j, P_k). $$

negatives.text: Let $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ be any set of points in the plane. Define $R(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n)$ as the radius of the smallest circle enclosing all these points. Show that when $n \ge 3$, there exist indices $i, j, k$ such that $$ R(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n) < R(P_i, P_j, P_k). $$

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle. Points $E$ and $F$ move along $AC$ and $AB$ respectively, satisfying $BC^2 = AB \cdot AF + CA \cdot CE$. Prove that the circle through $A$, $E$, and $F$ always contains a fixed point distinct from $A$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle. Points $E$ and $F$ move along $AC$ and $AB$ respectively, satisfying $BC^2 = AB \cdot AF - CA \cdot CE$. Prove that the circle through $A$, $E$, and $F$ always contains a fixed point distinct from $A$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$ inscribed in a circle $\omega$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $C$ intersects the line through $B$ parallel to $AC$ at a point $D$. The tangent of $c$ at $B$ meets the parallel from $C$ to $AB$ at the point $E$ and the tangent of $c$ at $C$ at the point $L$. positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB \neq AC$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$ and $\Gamma$ again at $E$. A circle with diameter $DE$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F$. Point $P$ lies on $AF$ such that $PB = PC$, and let $X$, $Y$ be the feet of perpendiculars from $P$ to $AB$ and $AC$.
