$$

positive_text: Soient $m, n$ deux entiers tels que $\mathrm{pgcd}(m, n)$ a au moins deux diviseurs premiers distincts. Soit $T=\{x \in \mathbb{N} \mid x \equiv m[n]\}$. Un élément de $T$ est dit irréductible s'il ne peut pas s'exprimer comme un produit d'au moins deux éléments de $T$ (pas nécessairement distincts). Montrer qu'il existe $K>0$ tel que tout élément de $T$ s'écrit comme produit d'au plus $K$ éléments irréductibles de $T$ (pas nécessairement distincts).

negatives.text: Soient $a, b$ deux entiers tels que $\mathrm{pgcd}(a, b)$ a exactement un facteur premier. Soit $S=\{x \in \mathbb{N} \mid x \equiv a[b]\}$. Un élément de $S$ est dit irréductible s'il ne peut pas s'écrire comme un produit d'au moins deux éléments de $S$ (pas forcément distincts). Montrer qu'il existe $N>0$ tel que tout élément de $S$ s'écrit comme produit d'au plus $N$ éléments irréductibles de $S$ (pas forcément distincts).

Soient $a, b$ deux entiers tels que $\mathrm{pgcd}(a, b)$ a au moins deux facteurs premiers distincts. Soit $S=\{x \in \mathbb{N} \mid x \equiv a[b]\}$. Montrer qu'il existe $N>0$ tel que tout élément de $S$ s'écrit comme somme d'au plus $N$ éléments irréductibles de $S$ (pas forcément distincts).

Soient $a, b$ deux entiers tels que $\mathrm{pgcd}(a, b)$ a au moins deux facteurs premiers distincts. Soit $S=\{x \in \mathbb{N} \mid x \equiv -a[b]\}$. Montrer qu'il existe $N>0$ tel que tout élément de $S$ s'écrit comme produit d'au plus $N$ éléments irréductibles de $S$ (pas forcément distincts).

positive_text: Soient $\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \ldots \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}$ des cercles de rayon égal, placés dans le plan de façon telle que deux cercles quelconques ne soient pas tangents et que l'ensemble des cercles forme une configuration connexe. Soit $S$ l'ensemble des points de croisement entre les cercles. Démontrer que le cardinal de $S$ est supérieur ou égal à $n$.

negatives.text: Soient $\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \ldots \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}$ des cercles de même rayon, placés dans le plan de sorte qu'ils ne soient jamais tangents 2 à 2 et qu'il existe toujours un chemin passant par les cercles pour aller d'un point de l'un d'entre eux à un autre. En notant $S$ l'ensemble des points d'intersection des cercles, montrer que $|S| \leqslant n$.

Soient $\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \ldots \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}$ des cercles de même rayon, placés dans le plan de sorte qu'ils ne soient jamais tangents 2 à 2 et qu'il existe toujours un chemin passant par les cercles pour aller d'un point de l'un d'entre eux à un autre. En notant $S$ l'ensemble des points d'intersection des cercles, montrer que $|S| = n$.

positive_text: Soit $ABC$ un triangle et soient $D$, $E$ et $F$ les points de contact respectifs du cercle $A$-exinscrit, noté $\omega_{A}$, avec le côté $BC$ et les demi-droites $[AC)$ et $[AB)$. Soit $M$ le milieu du segment $[E,F]$. La droite $(DM)$ recoupe le cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$. La tangente au cercle circonscrit au triangle $ABC$ au point $A$ et la tangente au cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$ se coupent en $R$. Démontrer que $RX = RM$.

negatives.text: Soit $ABC$ un triangle et soient $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$ et $C_{1}$ les points de contact respectifs du cercle $A$-exinscrit, noté $\omega_{A}$, avec le côté $BC$ et les demi-droites $[AC)$ et $[AB)$. positive_text: Soient $x$ et $y$ deux nombres réels. On suppose que $x^2 + 2x = y^2 + 2y$. Démontrer que si $x$ est un entier (positif, négatif ou nul), alors $y$ est également un entier.

negatives.text: Soient $a$ et $b$ deux réels. Supposons que $2a + a^{3} = 2b + b^{3}$. Montrer que si $a$ est un entier, alors $b$ est aussi un entier.

positive_text: Trouver tous les entiers positifs ou nuls $n$ tels que $n! + 2023$ est un carré.

negatives.text: Déterminer tous les entiers $n \geqslant 0$ tels que $2023 - n!$ est un carré parfait.
Trouver tous les entiers $n \geqslant 0$ tels que $2023 + n^2$ est un carré parfait.
Déterminer tous les entiers $n \geqslant 0$ tels que $2023 + n!$ est un cube parfait.

positive_text:

$$
\left(2 a^{2}+b c\right)\left(2 b^{2}+a c\right)\left(2 c^{2}+a b\right)=26 a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}
$$

$$

positive_text:

$$

$$

positive_text:

 x_{1}(1 - x_{2}),\ x_{2}(1 - x_{3}),\ \ldots,\ x_{n}(1 - x_{1})
$$

positive_text: Un entier $n \geqslant 2$ est inscrit sur un tableau. À chaque étape, un diviseur premier $p$ de $n$ est sélectionné, $n$ est remplacé par $n+\frac{n}{p}$. Démontrer que $p=3$ apparaît infiniment souvent dans la suite des choix effectués.

negatives.text: Un entier $n \geqslant 2$ est écrit au tableau. Chaque jour, quelqu'un choisit $p$ un diviseur premier de $n$, efface $n$ et écrit $n-\frac{n}{p}$ à la place. Montrer que $p=3$ est choisi une infinité de fois.

positive_text: Soient $x$, $y$, $z$ des nombres réels strictement positifs. Montrer que $$\frac{x}{1 + 9 y z} + \frac{y}{1 + 9 z x} + \frac{z}{1 + 9 x y} \geq \frac{x + y + z}{1 + (x + y + z)^2} .$$

negatives.text: Démontrer, pour tous réels $a$, $b$, $c$ strictement positifs, l'inégalité suivante : $$\frac{a}{9 b c-1} + \frac{b}{9 c a-1} + \frac{c}{9 a b-1} \geqslant \frac{a+b+c}{1+(a+b+c)^{2}} .$$

Démontrer, pour tous réels $a$, $b$, $c$ strictement positifs, l'inégalité suivante : $$\frac{a}{9 b c+1} + \frac{b}{9 c a+1} + \frac{c}{9 a b+1} \leqslant \frac{a+b+c}{1+(a+b+c)^{2}} .$$

positive_text: Soient $x, y, z$ trois réels strictement positifs. Montrer que $$\frac{x^{4}+1}{y^{3}+y^{2}+y}+\frac{y^{4}+1}{z^{3}+z^{2}+z}+\frac{z^{4}+1}{x^{3}+x^{2}+x} \geqslant 2$$

negatives.text: Soient $a, b, c$ trois réels strictement positifs. Montrer que $$\frac{a^{4}-1}{b^{3}+b^{2}+b}+\frac{b^{4}-1}{c^{3}+c^{2}+c}+\frac{c^{4}-1}{a^{3}+a^{2}+a} \geqslant 2$$

Soient $a, b, c$ trois réels strictement positifs. Montrer que $$\frac{a^{4}+1}{b^{2}+b+1}+\frac{b^{4}+1}{c^{2}+c+1}+\frac{c^{4}+1}{a^{2}+a+1} \geqslant 2$$

positive_text: Soient $x, y, z, w$ quatre réels tels que $|x| > 1$, $|y| > 1$, $|z| > 1$ et $|w| > 1$. Supposons que $(x+1)(y+1)(z+1)(w+1) = (x-1)(y-1)(z-1)(w-1)$. Montrer que $$\frac{1}{x-1} + \frac{1}{y-1} + \frac{1}{z-1} + \frac{1}{w-1} > 0$$

positive_text:
Soit $n \geqslant 1$ un entier et $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}$ des réels strictement positifs. Montrer que
$$
\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{a_k}{k} \right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k a_k \right) \leqslant \frac{(n+1)^2}{4n} \left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k \right)^2
$$
Pour quelles valeurs d'égalité est-ce atteint?

negatives.text:

$$

$$

positive_text: Die Zahlen $1$ bis $n^{2}$ werden zufällig in einem $n \times n$-Raster platziert ($n \geq 2$). Bestimmen Sie den größtmöglichen Wert von $C$.

Für jedes Paar von Zahlen innerhalb einer Zeile oder Spalte berechnen wir die Differenz $\max(a,b) - \min(a,b)$. Die Charakteristik $C$ sei der minimale solche Wert. Bestimmen Sie den größtmöglichen Wert von $C$.

positive_text: Bestimme alle positiven ganzen Zahlen $n$ mit folgender Eigenschaft: Die rekursive Folge $b_{0}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots$ mit $b_{0}=\frac{2n+1}{2}$ und $b_{k+1}=b_{k}\cdot\left\lfloor b_{k}\right\rfloor$ für $k \geq 0$ enthält mindestens einen ganzzahligen Wert.

negatives.text: Bestimme alle positiven ganzen Zahlen $m$ mit folgender Eigenschaft: Die Folge $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ mit $a_{0}=\frac{2m-1}{2}$ und $a_{k+1}=a_{k}\left\lfloor a_{k}\right\rfloor$ für $k=0,1,2, \ldots$ enthält wenigstens eine ganze Zahl.

positive_text: Seien $a$ und $b$ positive ganze Zahlen mit $b > a$. Ein Binärstring der Länge $b$ ist eine Abfolge von $b$ Zeichen, wobei jedes entweder 0 oder 1 ist. Anja wählt einen solchen Binärstring aus. Danach notiert sie alle Binärstrings, die sich an genau $a$ Stellen von ihrem ausgewählten String unterscheiden, an die Tafel. Später betritt Bernhard den Raum. Anja teilt ihm den Wert von $a$ mit, und Bernhard analysiert die Tafel. Welche minimale Anzahl an Versuchen braucht Bernhard, um den ursprünglichen Binärstring mit Sicherheit zu identifizieren? (In Abhängigkeit von $a$ und $b$)

negatives.text: Gegeben seien positive ganze Zahlen $k$ und $n$ mit $n>k$. Anja wählt ein Binärwort der Länge $n$ aus. Danach schreibt sie alle Binärwörter an die Tafel, die sich an mindestens $k$ Stellen von ihrem ursprünglichen Wort unterscheiden. Bernhard betritt den Raum, erfährt den Wert von $k$ und versucht, das ursprüngliche Binärwort zu erraten. Was ist die minimale Anzahl an Versuchen, die Bernhard benötigt, um es mit Sicherheit zu erraten?

Gegeben seien positive ganze Zahlen $k$ und $n$ mit $n>k$. Anja wählt ein Binärwort der Länge $n$ aus. Danach schreibt sie alle Binärwörter an die Tafel, die sich an maximal $k$ Stellen von ihrem ursprünglichen Wort unterscheiden. Bernhard betritt den Raum, erfährt den Wert von $k$ und versucht, das ursprüngliche Binärwort zu erraten. Was ist die minimale Anzahl an Versuchen, die Bernhard benötigt, um es mit Sicherheit zu erraten?

Gegeben seien positive ganze Zahlen $k$ und $n$ mit $n>k$. Anja wählt ein Binärwort der Länge $n$ aus. Danach schreibt sie alle Binärwörter an die Tafel, die sich an $k$ aufeinanderfolgenden Stellen von ihrem ursprünglichen Wort unterscheiden. Bernhard betritt den Raum, erfährt den Wert von $k$ und versucht, das ursprüngliche Binärwort zu erraten. Was ist die minimale Anzahl an Versuchen, die Bernhard benötigt, um es mit Sicherheit zu erraten?

positive_text: Sei $k$ eine positive ganze Zahl und $\left(b_{n}\right)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ eine Folge positiver ganzer Zahlen, in der jede positive ganze Zahl genau einmal vorkommt. Angenommen, es gilt $\left|b_{n+1} - b_{n}\right| \leq 2k$ für alle $n > 10^{100}$. Zeigen Sie, dass unendlich viele natürliche Zahlen $m$ existieren mit $\left|b_{m} - m\right| < k$.

negatives.text: Es sei $d$ eine positive ganze Zahl und $\left(a_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{\infty}$ eine Folge positiver ganzer Zahlen, in der jede positive ganze Zahl genau einmal vorkommt. Angenommen, es gilt $\left|a_{i+1} - a_{i}\right| \leq 2d$ für alle $i \geq 10^{100}$. Zeigen Sie, dass unendlich viele Indizes $j$ existieren mit $\left|a_{j} + j\right| < d$.

Es sei $d$ eine positive ganze Zahl und $\left(a_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{\infty}$ eine Folge positiver ganzer Zahlen, in der jede positive ganze Zahl genau einmal vorkommt. Angenommen, es gilt $\left|a_{i+1} - a_{i}\right| \leq 2d$ für alle $i \geq 10^{100}$. Zeigen Sie, dass unendlich viele Indizes $j$ existieren mit $\left|a_{j} - j\right| < 2d$.

positive_text: Bestimmen Sie, ob eine Menge $M$ von natürlichen Zahlen existiert, für die gilt: Zu jeder positiven rationalen Zahl $r$ mit $r < 1$ gibt es genau eine endliche Teilmenge $S \subseteq M$, sodass $\sum_{s \in S} \frac{1}{s} = r$ ist.

negatives.text: Entscheiden Sie, ob es eine Menge $M$ positiver ganzer Zahlen gibt, die folgende Eigenschaft hat: Für jede positive rationale Zahl $r<1$ existiert genau eine endliche Teilmenge $S$ von $M$, sodass $\sum_{s \in S} 1 / s^2 = r$ gilt.

Entscheiden Sie, ob es eine Menge $M$ positiver ganzer Zahlen gibt, die folgende Eigenschaft hat: Für jede positive rationale Zahl $r<1$ existiert genau eine unendliche Teilmenge $S$ von $M$, sodass $\sum_{s \in S} 1 / s = r$ gilt.

Entscheiden Sie, ob es eine Menge $M$ positiver ganzer Zahlen gibt, die folgende Eigenschaft hat: Für jede positive rationale Zahl $r<1$ existiert genau eine endliche Teilmenge $S$ von $M$, sodass $\sum_{s \in S} s = r$ gilt.

positive_text: Sei $\delta > 0$ vorgegeben. Zeigen Sie, dass es ganze Zahlen $x, y$ und $z$, nicht alle null, gibt, mit $|x \sqrt{2} + y \sqrt{3} + z \sqrt{5}| < \delta$. Beweisen Sie ferner, dass jedes solche Tripel $(x, y, z) \neq (0,0,0)$, das die Ungleichung erfüllt, mindestens einen der Werte $|x|, |y|, |z|$ besitzt, der größer als $\delta^{-1 / 3} / \sqrt{30}$ ist.

negatives.text: Sei $\varepsilon > 0$ gegeben. Zeigen Sie, dass es ganze Zahlen $a, b$ und $c$, nicht alle null, gibt, mit $|a \sqrt{2} + b \sqrt{3} + c \sqrt{5}| > \varepsilon$. Beweisen Sie auch, dass jedes solche Tripel $(a, b, c) \neq (0,0,0)$ mindestens einen der Absolutbeträge $|a|, |b|, |c|$ besitzt, der kleiner als $\varepsilon^{-1 / 3} / \sqrt{30}$ ist.

Sei $\varepsilon > 0$ gegeben. Zeigen Sie, dass es ganze Zahlen $a, b$ und $c$, nicht alle null, gibt, mit $|a \sqrt{2} + b \sqrt{3} + c \sqrt{5}| < \varepsilon$. Beweisen Sie außerdem, dass in jedem solchen Tripel $(a, b, c) \neq (0,0,0)$, das die Ungleichung erfüllt, mindestens einer der Absolutbeträge $|a|, |b|, |c|$ größer als $\varepsilon^{-1 / 2} / \sqrt{30}$ ist.

Sei $\varepsilon > 0$ gegeben. Zeigen Sie, dass es ganze Zahlen $a, b$ und $c$, nicht alle null, gibt, mit $|a \sqrt{2} + b \sqrt{3} + c \sqrt{5}| < \varepsilon$. Beweisen Sie ferner, dass jedes solche Tripel $(a, b, c) \neq (0,0,0)$, das die Ungleichung erfüllt, mindestens einen der Absolutbeträge $|a|, |b|, |c|$ besitzt, der größer als $\varepsilon^{-1 / 3} / 2$ ist.

positive_text: Beweisen Sie, dass für jede nichtnegative ganze Zahl $z$ eindeutig ein geordnetes Paar $(a, b)$ positiver ganzer Zahlen $a, b$ existiert, mit $2 z = (a + b)^2 - a - 3 b$.

negatives.text: Beweisen Sie, dass es für jede nichtnegative ganze Zahl $z$ genau ein geordnetes Paar $(m, n)$ positiver ganzer Zahlen $m, n$ gibt, so dass $2 z = (m+n)^2 + m - 3 n$ gilt.
Beweisen Sie, dass es für jede nichtnegative ganze Zahl $z$ genau ein geordnetes Paar $(m, n)$ positiver ganzer Zahlen $m, n$ gibt, so dass $2 z = (m+n)^2 - m - 3 n^2$ gilt.
Beweisen Sie, dass es für jede nichtnegative ganze Zahl $z$ genau ein geordnetes Paar $(m, n)$ positiver ganzer Zahlen $m, n$ gibt, so dass $2 z = (m+n)^2 - m - 3 n$ und $m > 2$ gilt.

positive_text: Gegeben sei ein gleichschenkliges Dreieck $ABC$ mit $\overline{BC} = \overline{CA}$. Ein Punkt $D$ liegt im Inneren der Seite $AB$ mit $\overline{AD} < \overline{DB}$. Die Punkte $P$ und $Q$ liegen innerhalb der Seiten $BC$ beziehungsweise $CA$, sodass $\angle DPB = \angle AQD = 90^\circ$. Die Mittelsenkrechte der Strecke $PQ$ schneidet $CQ$ in $E$, und die Umkreise von $ABC$ und $QPC$ haben einen gemeinsamen Punkt $F$ außer $C$. Zeigen Sie: Ist $P$, $E$ und $F$ kollinear, dann folgt $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$.
Sei $m$ eine positive ganze Zahl und $A$ eine Menge mit $4m+1$ Elementen aus $\{0,1,2, \ldots, 5^{m}\}$. Zeigen Sie, dass es drei Elemente $x, y, z$ in $A$ gibt, sodass $x < y < z$ und $z + 2x > 3y$.

negatives.text: Für eine positive ganze Zahl $m$ sei $A$ eine Teilmenge von $\{0,1,2, \ldots, 5^{m}\}$ mit $4m+1$ Elementen. Zeigen Sie, dass es drei Zahlen $a, b, c$ in $A$ gibt, sodass $a < b < c$ und $c + 2a < 3b$ gilt.

Für eine positive ganze Zahl $m$ sei $A$ eine Teilmenge von $\{0,1,2, \ldots, 5^{m}\}$ mit $4m+1$ Elementen. Zeigen Sie, dass es drei Zahlen $a, b, c$ in $A$ gibt, sodass $a < b < c$ und $c + a > 3b$ gilt.

Für eine positive ganze Zahl $m$ sei $A$ eine Teilmenge von $\{0,1,2, \ldots, 5^{m}\}$ mit $4m+1$ Elementen. Zeigen Sie, dass es drei Zahlen $a, b, c$ in $A$ gibt, sodass $a < b < c$ und $c^2 + 2a > 3b$ gilt.

positive_text: Es sei $ABCD$ ein Parallelogramm mit $|AC| = |BC|$. Ein Punkt $P$ liege auf dem Strahl $AB$ mit $B$ zwischen $A$ und $P$. Der Kreis durch $A$, $C$, $D$ schneide die Strecke $PD$ in einem weiteren Punkt $Q$ außer $D$. Der Kreis durch $A$, $P$, $Q$ schneide die Strecke $PC$ in einem weiteren Punkt $R$ außer $P$. Zeigen Sie, dass die Geraden $CD$, $AQ$ und $BR$ konkurrent sind.

negatives.text: Es sei $ABCD$ ein Parallelogramm mit $|AC| = |BD|$. Ein Punkt $P$ liege auf dem Strahl $AB$ mit $B$ zwischen $A$ und $P$. Der Umkreis des Dreiecks $ACD$ und die Strecke $PD$ haben außer $D$ noch den Punkt $Q$ gemeinsam. Der Umkreis des Dreiecks $APQ$ und die Strecke $PC$ haben außer $P$ noch den Punkt $R$ gemeinsam. Beweisen Sie, dass sich $CD$, $AQ$ und $BR$ in einem Punkt schneiden.

Es sei $ABCD$ ein Parallelogramm mit $|AC| = |BC|$. Ein Punkt $P$ liege auf dem Strahl $AB$ mit $B$ zwischen $A$ und $P$. Der Umkreis des Dreiecks $ACD$ und die Strecke $PD$ haben außer $D$ noch den Punkt $Q$ gemeinsam. Der Umkreis des Dreiecks $APQ$ und die Strecke $PC$ haben außer $P$ noch den Punkt $R$ gemeinsam. Beweisen Sie, dass sich $AD$, $AQ$ und $BR$ in einem Punkt schneiden.

Es sei $ABCD$ ein Parallelogramm mit $|AC| = |BC|$. Ein Punkt $P$ liege auf dem Strahl $AB$ mit $B$ zwischen $A$ und $P$. Der Umkreis des Dreiecks $ACD$ und die Strecke $PD$ haben außer $D$ noch den Punkt $Q$ gemeinsam. Der Umkreis des Dreiecks $APQ$ und die Strecke $PC$ haben außer $P$ noch den Punkt $R$ gemeinsam. Beweisen Sie, dass sich $CD$, $AR$ und $BP$ in einem Punkt schneiden.

positive_text:
In triangle $AB\Gamma$, it is given that $\angle A = 105°$ and $\angle \Gamma = \frac{1}{4}\angle B$.

α. Find the measures of $\angle B$ and $\angle \Gamma$.

β. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AB\Gamma$, and let $\Delta$ be the point diametrically opposite to $B$. Show that the perpendicular distance from $\Gamma$ to line $B\Delta$ equals $\frac{1}{4}B\Delta$.

negatives.text:
A triangle $AB\Gamma$ is given with $\angle A = 105°$ and $\angle \Gamma = \frac{\angle B}{3}$.

α. Determine the measures of $\angle B$ and $\angle \Gamma$.

β. If $O$ is the center of the circumcircle of the triangle $AB\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ is the antipodal of $B$, prove that the distance of $\Gamma$ from $B\Delta$ is $\frac{B\Delta}{4}$.

A triangle $AB\Gamma$ is given with $\angle A = 105°$ and $\angle \Gamma = \frac{\angle B}{4}$.

α. Determine the measures of $\angle B$ and $\angle \Gamma$.

β. If $O$ is the center of the circumcircle of the triangle $AB\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ is the point such that $\angle B\Delta O = 90°$, prove that the distance of $\Gamma$ from $B\Delta$ is $\frac{B\Delta}{4}$.

positive_text: Given two concentric circles with outer radius $11r$ and inner radius $9r$, place as many non-overlapping circles of radius $r$ as possible such that each is tangent to both the inner and outer boundaries. Use the approximation $9.94 < \sqrt{99} < 9.95$ to help in your calculation.

negatives.text: In a circular ring with radii $R$ and $R - 2r$, where $R = 10r$, we put non-overlapping circles of radius $r$ tangent to the circles defining the circular ring. Determine the maximal number of these circles. (It is given that $9.94 < \sqrt{99} < 9.95$)

In a circular ring with radii $R$ and $R - 2r$, where $R = 11r$, we put non-overlapping circles of radius $r$ tangent to the outer boundary and intersecting the inner boundary. Determine the maximal number of these circles. (It is given that $9.94 < \sqrt{99} < 9.95$)

positive_text: Determine all integers $ x $ such that $ \frac{9x^2 + 31}{x^2 + 7} $ is an integer.

negatives.text: If the number $ K = \frac{9n^2 + 31}{n^2 - 7} $ is integer, find the possible values of $ n \in \mathbb{Z} $.
If the number $ K = \frac{9n^2 + 31}{n^3 + 7} $ is integer, find the possible values of $ n \in \mathbb{Z} $.
If the number $ K = \frac{9n^2 - 31}{n^2 + 7} $ is integer, find the possible values of $ n \in \mathbb{Z} $.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have circumcenter $O$, and let $D, E, F$ be the midpoints of $BC, AC$, and $AB$, respectively. Define points $D', E', F'$ such that $\overrightarrow{OD'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OD}$, $\overrightarrow{OE'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OE}$, and $\overrightarrow{OF'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OF}$ for some $\lambda > 0$. Prove that the lines $AD', BE', CF'$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have circumcenter $O$, and let $D, E, F$ be the midpoints of $BC, AC$, and $AB$, respectively. Define points $D', E', F'$ such that $\overrightarrow{OD'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OD} + \overrightarrow{O}$, $\overrightarrow{OE'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OE} + \overrightarrow{O}$, and $\overrightarrow{OF'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OF} + \overrightarrow{O}$ for some $\lambda > 0$. Prove that the lines $AD', BE', CF'$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ have circumcenter $O$, and let $D, E, F$ be the midpoints of $BC, AC$, and $AB$, respectively. Define points $D', E', F'$ such that $\overrightarrow{OD'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OD} + \overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{OE'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OE} + \overrightarrow{BC}$, and $\overrightarrow{OF'} = \lambda \cdot \overrightarrow{OF} + \overrightarrow{CA}$ for some $\lambda > 0$. Prove that the lines $AD', BE', CF'$ are concurrent.

positive_text:
\text{Let } z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4, z_5, z_6 \text{ be six distinct complex numbers such that their corresponding points } A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4, A_5, A_6 \text{ lie consecutively on a circle centered at the origin with radius } r > 0. Let } w \text{ be a root of } z^2 + z + 1 = 0. Suppose that}\\
\quad z_1 w^2 + z_3 w + z_5 = 0 \quad (I),\\
\quad z_2 w^2 + z_4 w + z_6 = 0 \quad (II).\\
\text{Show that: (a) triangle } A_1A_3A_5 \text{ is equilateral,}\\
\quad |z_1 - z_2| + |z_2 - z_3| + |z_3 - z_4| + |z_4 - z_5| + |z_5 - z_6| + |z_6 - z_1| = 3|z_1 - z_4| = 3|z_2 - z_5| = 3|z_3 - z_6|.

negatives.text:
\text{Let } z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4, z_5, z_6 \text{ be six distinct complex numbers with images } A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4, A_5, A_6 \text{ lying consecutively on a circle centered at the origin with radius } r > 0. Let } w \text{ be a root of } z^2 - z + 1 = 0. Suppose that}\\
\quad z_1 w^2 + z_3 w + z_5 = 0 \quad (I),\\
\quad z_2 w^2 + z_4 w + z_6 = 0 \quad (II).\\
\text{Prove that: (a) the triangle } A_1A_3A_5 \text{ is equilateral,}\\
\quad |z_1 - z_2| + |z_2 - z_3| + |z_3 - z_4| + |z_4 - z_5| + |z_5 - z_6| + |z_6 - z_1| = 3|z_1 - z_4| = 3|z_2 - z_5| = 3|z_3 - z_6|.

\text{Let } z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4, z_5, z_6 \text{ be six distinct complex numbers whose images } A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4, A_5, A_6 \text{ are consecutive points on a circle with center } O(0,0) \text{ and radius } r > 0. Let } w \text{ be a root of } z^2 + z + 1 = 0. Suppose that}\\
\quad z_1 w + z_3 w^2 + z_5 = 0 \quad (I),\\
\quad z_2 w + z_4 w^2 + z_6 = 0 \quad (II).\\
\text{Prove that: (a) the triangle } A_1A_3A_5 \text{ is equilateral,}\\
\quad |z_1 - z_2| + |z_2 - z_3| + |z_3 - z_4| + |z_4 - z_5| + |z_5 - z_6| + |z_6 - z_1| = 3|z_1 - z_4| = 3|z_2 - z_5| = 3|z_3 - z_6|.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a scalene triangle with $AB < AC$, with circumcircle $\omega$. A circle centered at $A$ with radius $AB$ intersects side $BC$ at $E$ and $\omega$ at $F$. The line $EF$ intersects $\omega$ again at $D$ and side $AC$ at $M$. The line $AD$ intersects side $BC$ at $K$. The circumcircle of $\triangle BKD$ intersects $AB$ again at $L$. Prove that $K, L, M$ are collinear and that the line through them is parallel to $BF$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a scalene triangle with $AB < AC$, with circumcircle $c$. A circle centered at $A$ with radius $AC$ intersects side $BC$ at $E$ and $c$ at $F$. The line $EF$ intersects $c$ again at $D$ and side $AC$ at $M$. The line $AD$ intersects side $BC$ at $K$. The circumcircle of $\triangle BKD$ intersects $AB$ at $L$. Prove that the points $K, L, M$ lie on a line parallel to $BF$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a scalene triangle with $AB < AC$, with circumcircle $c$. A circle centered at $A$ with radius $AB$ intersects side $BC$ at $E$ and $c$ at $F$. The line $EF$ intersects $c$ again at $D$ and side $AC$ at $M$. The line $AD$ intersects side $BC$ at $K$. The circumcircle of $\triangle BKC$ intersects $AB$ at $L$. Prove that the points $K, L, M$ lie on a line parallel to $BF$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a scalene triangle with $AB < AC$, with circumcircle $c$. A circle centered at $A$ with radius $AB$ intersects side $BC$ at $E$ and $c$ at $F$. The line $EF$ intersects $c$ again at $D$ and side $AC$ at $M$. The line $AD$ intersects side $BC$ at $K$. The circumcircle of $\triangle BKD$ intersects $AB$ at $L$. positive_text:
Determine all integer pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying the equation
$$
a^3 b^2 (2b - a) = a^2 b^4 - 36.
$$

negatives.text:

$$
x^3 y^2 (2y + x) = x^2 y^4 - 36.
$$

Solve in the set of integers the equation

x^3 y^2 (2y - x) = x^2 y^4 + 36.

positive_text: Let $S$ be a finite set of positive real numbers, define $D = \left\{\frac{a}{b}: a, b \in S\right\}$ and $E = \left\{ab: a, b \in S\right\}$. If $|S|$ denotes the cardinality of $S$, prove that $|S| \cdot |D| \le |E|^2$.

negatives.text: Let $A$ be a finite set of positive reals, let $B = \left\{\frac{x}{y}: x, y \in A\right\}$ and let $C = \left\{xy: x, y \in A\right\}$. If $|A|$ denotes the size of $A$, show that $|A| \cdot |C| \le |B|^2$.

Let $A$ be a finite set of positive reals, let $B = \left\{\frac{x}{y}: x, y \in A\right\}$ and let $C = \left\{x + y: x, y \in A\right\}$. If $|A|$ denotes the size of $A$, prove that $|A| \cdot |B| \le |C|^2$.

Let $A$ be a finite set of positive reals, let $B = \left\{\frac{x}{y}: x, y \in A, x \ne y\right\}$ and let $C = \left\{xy: x, y \in A\right\}$. If $|A|$ denotes the size of $A$, prove that $|A| \cdot |B| \le |C|^2$.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a + b + c = 12$. Show that:
$$
\frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a} + 3 \ge \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c}.
$$
**For which values of $a$, $b$, $c$ does equality hold?**

negatives.text:
If $x$, $y$, $z$ are positive real numbers with sum $12$, prove that:
$$
\frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{x} - 3 \ge \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z}.
$$

If $x$, $y$, $z$ are positive real numbers with sum $12$, prove that:
$$
\frac{x^2}{y} + \frac{y^2}{z} + \frac{z^2}{x} + 3 \ge \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z}.
$$

If $x$, $y$, $z$ are positive real numbers with sum $12$, prove that:
$$
\frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{x} + 3 \le \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z}.
$$

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle centered at $O$ with radius $R$. A circle centered at $B$ with radius $AB$ intersects $AC$ at $K$ and the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $E$. The line $KE$ intersects the circumcircle again at $F$. The line $BO$ meets $KE$ at $L$ and $AC$ at $M$. The intersection of $AE$ and $BF$ is $D$. Prove that the quadrilateral $DLMF$ and the pentagon $BDKME$ lie on a circle each.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in the circle $c(O, R)$. The circle $c_1(B, AB)$ intersects the side $AC$ at point $K$ and the circle $c$ at point $E$. The line $KE$ intersects the circle $c$ also at point $F$. The line $AO$ intersects $KE$ at point $L$ and $AC$ at point $M$. Finally, the line $AE$ intersects $BF$ at point $D$. Prove that the polygons $DLMF$ and $BDKME$ are cyclic.

Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in the circle $c(O, R)$. The circle $c_1(B, AB)$ intersects the side $AC$ at point $K$ and the circle $c$ at point $E$. The line $KE$ intersects the circle $c$ also at point $F$. The line $BO$ intersects $KE$ at point $L$ and $AB$ at point $M$. Finally, the line $AE$ intersects $BF$ at point $D$. Prove that the polygons $DLMF$ and $BDKME$ are cyclic.

positive_text: Prove that $\left(x+2y+\frac{2}{x+1}\right)\left(y+2x+\frac{2}{y+1}\right) \ge 16$, for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$ with $xy \ge 1$.

negatives.text: Show that $\left(a+2b+\frac{2}{a+1}\right)\left(b+2a+\frac{2}{b+1}\right) \le 16$, for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $ab \ge 1$.
Show that $\left(a+2b+\frac{2}{a^2+1}\right)\left(b+2a+\frac{2}{b^2+1}\right) \ge 16$, for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $ab \ge 1$.

positive_text: Let $N = wxyz = w \cdot 10^3 + x \cdot 10^2 + y \cdot 10 + z$ be a four-digit positive integer such that $w \ge 7$ and $w > x > y > z > 0$. Define $M = \overline{zyxw} = z \cdot 10^3 + y \cdot 10^2 + x \cdot 10 + w$. If all digits of $N + M$ are odd, find all possible values of $N$.

negatives.text: Let $A = abcd = a \cdot 10^3 + b \cdot 10^2 + c \cdot 10 + d$ be a four-digit positive integer such that $a \ge 7$ and $a > b > c > d > 0$. Let $B = \overline{dcba} = d \cdot 10^3 + c \cdot 10^2 + b \cdot 10 + a$. If all digits of $A - B$ are odd, determine all possible values of $A$.

Let $A = abcd = a \cdot 10^3 + b \cdot 10^2 + c \cdot 10 + d$ be a four-digit positive integer such that $a \ge 7$ and $a > b > c > d > 0$. Let $B = \overline{dcba} = d \cdot 10^3 + c \cdot 10^2 + b \cdot 10 + a$. If all digits of $A + B$ are even, determine all possible values of $A$.

Let $A = abcd = a \cdot 10^3 + b \cdot 10^2 + c \cdot 10 + d$ be a four-digit positive integer such that $a \ge 7$ and $a > b > c > d > 0$. Let $B = \overline{dcba} = d \cdot 10^3 + c \cdot 10^2 + b \cdot 10 + a$. If the sum $A + B$ is divisible by 11, determine all possible values of $A$.

positive_text:
In a mathematical competition, some participants are friends; the friendship relation is symmetric. A sequence of $n \ge 3$ participants $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ is called a weekly-friendly cycle if $X_i$ is not friends with $X_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i \le n$ (where $X_{n+1} = X_1$), and there are no other non-friend pairs among the members of the sequence.

It is given that for every participant $P$, and every weekly-friendly cycle $\mathcal{X}$ not containing $P$, the set of participants in $\mathcal{X}$ who are not friends with $P$ has at most one element.

Prove that all participants can be partitioned into three groups such that any two participants in the same group are friends.

negatives.text:
In a mathematical competition, some participants are friends; the friendship relation is symmetric. A sequence of $n \ge 3$ participants $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ is called a weekly-friendly circle if $X_i$ is not friends with $X_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i \le n$ (where $X_{n+1} = X_1$), and there are no other non-friend pairs among the members of the sequence.

positive_text: \text{Determine all positive integer solutions } (x, y, z) \text{ to the equation: } \frac{1}{x} + \frac{2}{y} = 1 + \frac{4}{z}

negatives.text: \text{Find all triads } (x, y, z) \text{ of positive integers satisfying the equation: } \frac{1}{x} - \frac{2}{y} - \frac{4}{z} = 1
\text{Find all triads } (x, y, z) \text{ of positive integers satisfying the equation: } \frac{1}{x} + \frac{2}{y} - \frac{4}{z^2} = 1
\text{Find all triads } (x, y, z) \text{ of positive integers satisfying the equation: } \frac{1}{x} + \frac{2}{y} - \frac{4}{z} = 2

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Outside the triangle, a parallelogram $BCDE$ is constructed so that $BE$ is parallel to $AM$ and $BE = \frac{1}{2} AM$. Show that the segment $EM$ goes through the midpoint of $AD$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle and let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Externally of the triangle we consider a parallelogram $BCDE$, such that $BE \parallel AM$ and $BE = 2AM$. Prove that the line $EM$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $AD$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle and let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Externally of the triangle we consider a parallelogram $BCDE$, such that $BE \parallel AM$ and $BE = AM / 2$. Prove that the line $ED$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $AD$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle and let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Externally of the triangle we consider a parallelogram $BCDE$, such that $BE \parallel AM$ and $BE = AM$. Prove that the line $EM$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $AD$.

positive_text:
Let $P(x) = a x^3 + (b - a) x^2 - (b + c) x + c$, $Q(x) = x^4 + (b - 1) x^3 + (a - b) x^2 - (a + c) x + c$ be polynomials of the indeterminate $x$, where $a, b, c$ are nonzero real numbers and $b > 0$. If the polynomial $P(x)$ has three distinct real roots $x_0, x_1, x_2$, which are also roots of the polynomial $Q(x)$, then:
(a) Prove that: $abc > 28$.
(b) If $a, b, c$ are nonzero integers with $b > 0$, find their possible values.

negatives.text:
Let $P(x) = a x^3 + (b - a) x^2 - (c + b) x + c$, $Q(x) = x^4 + (b + 1) x^3 + (a - b) x^2 - (c + a) x + c$ be polynomials of the indeterminate $x$, where $a, b, c$ are nonzero real numbers and $b > 0$. If the polynomial $P(x)$ has three different real roots $x_0, x_1, x_2$, which are also roots of the polynomial $Q(x)$, then:
(a) Prove that: $abc > 28$.
(b) If $a, b, c$ are nonzero integers with $b > 0$, find their possible values.

Let $P(x) = a x^3 + (b - a) x^2 - (c + b) x + c$, $Q(x) = x^4 + (b - 1) x^3 + (a - b) x^2 - (c + a) x + c$ be polynomials of the indeterminate $x$, where $a, b, c$ are nonzero real numbers and $b < 0$. If the polynomial $P(x)$ has three different real roots $x_0, x_1, x_2$, which are also roots of the polynomial $Q(x)$, then:
(a) Prove that: $abc > 28$.
(b) If $a, b, c$ are nonzero integers with $b > 0$, find their possible values.

positive_text: Find all nonnegative integer pairs $(a, b)$, $a \ge b$, such that $(a+b)^3$ divides $2b(3a^2 + b^2) + 8$.

negatives.text: Find all nonnegative integer pairs $(m, n)$, $m \ge n$, such that $(m+n)^3$ divides $2n(3m^2 - n^2) + 8$.
Find all nonnegative integer pairs $(m, n)$, $m \ge n$, such that $(m+n)^3$ divides $2n(3m^2 + n^2) - 8$.
Find all nonnegative integer pairs $(m, n)$, $m \ge n$, such that $(m+n)^3$ divides $2n(3m^2 + n^2) + 9$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$ and circumcenter $O$. The altitudes from $B$ and $C$ intersect at point $H$. If $O_1$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BHC$, prove that the quadrilateral $AHO_1O$ is a parallelogram.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$ and circumcenter $O$. The altitudes from $B$ and $C$ intersect at point $H$. If $O_1$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BHC$, prove that the quadrilateral $AHO_1O$ is a rectangle.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$ and circumcenter $O$. The altitudes from $B$ and $C$ intersect at point $H$. If $O_1$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BHC$, prove that the quadrilateral $AHO_1O$ is cyclic.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB \le AC$ and $\omega$ its circumcircle. A line is drawn from $A$, perpendicular to the tangent to $\omega$ at $C$, meeting it at point $D$.

(α) If triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$, show that: $CD = \frac{BC}{2}$.

(β) If $CD = \frac{BC}{2}$, show that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

negatives.text:
Let $AB\Gamma$ be an acute triangle with $AB \le A\Gamma$ and $c(O, R)$ its circumcircle. A line is drawn from $A$ parallel to the tangent of $c(O, R)$ at $\Gamma$, intersecting the tangent at $\Delta$.

(α) If triangle $AB\Gamma$ is isosceles with $AB = A\Gamma$, prove that: $\Gamma\Delta = \frac{B\Gamma}{2}$.

(β) If $\Gamma\Delta = \frac{B\Gamma}{2}$, prove that triangle $AB\Gamma$ is isosceles.

Let $AB\Gamma$ be an acute triangle with $AB \le A\Gamma$ and $c(O, R)$ its circumcircle. The line perpendicular from $A$ to the tangent of $c(O, R)$ at $\Gamma$ intersects it at $\Delta$.

(α) If triangle $AB\Gamma$ is isosceles with $AB = A\Gamma$, prove that: $\Gamma\Delta = \frac{\Gamma B^2}{2}$.

(β) If $\Gamma\Delta = \frac{\Gamma B^2}{2}$, prove that triangle $AB\Gamma$ is isosceles.

Let $AB\Gamma$ be an acute triangle with $AB \le A\Gamma$ and $c(O, R)$ its circumcircle. The line perpendicular from $A$ to the tangent of $c(O, R)$ at $\Gamma$ intersects it at $\Delta$.

(α) If triangle $AB\Gamma$ is isosceles with $AB = A\Gamma$, prove that: $\Gamma\Delta = \frac{B\Gamma}{3}$.

(β) If $\Gamma\Delta = \frac{B\Gamma}{3}$, prove that triangle $AB\Gamma$ is isosceles.

positive_text: Let $x > 0$ be a real number. Show that: $x^3 - 3x + 2 \ge 0$. Given real numbers $x, y, z > 0$, prove the inequality: $$\frac{x^2 y}{z} + \frac{y^2 z}{x} + \frac{z^2 x}{y} + 2 \left( \frac{y}{xz} + \frac{z}{xy} + \frac{x}{yz} \right) \ge 9.$$(1) Determine the condition for equality.

Let $ABCD$ be a square with side length $\alpha$. Points $E$ and $Z$ lie on side $AD$ such that $DE = \frac{\alpha}{3}$ and $AZ = \frac{\alpha}{4}$. If the lines $BZ$ and $CE$ intersect at point $H$, find the area of triangle $BC H$ in terms of $\alpha$.

negatives.text: Let $AB\Gamma\Delta$ be a square of side $\alpha$. Points $E$ and $Z$ lie on side $A\Gamma\Delta$ such that $\Delta E = \frac{\alpha}{3}$ and $AZ = -\frac{\alpha}{4}$. If the lines $BZ$ and $\Gamma E$ intersect at point $H$, find the area of triangle $B\Gamma H$ as a function of $\alpha$.

Let $AB\Gamma\Delta$ be a square of side $\alpha$. Points $E$ and $Z$ lie on side $A\Gamma\Delta$ such that $\Delta E = \frac{\alpha}{3}$ and $AZ = \frac{\alpha}{4}$. If the lines $BZ$ and $\Gamma E$ intersect at point $H$, find the area of triangle $B\Gamma H$ as a function of $\alpha^2$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle $c$ with center $O$. Let $G$ denote the centroid and $D, E, F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A, B, C$, respectively. Suppose the lines $AG$ and $GD$ meet $c$ again at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Show that $F, E, M, N$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle $c$ of center $O$. Let $G$ be its barycenter and $D, E, F$ the foot of the altitudes from $A, B, C$, respectively. If the rays $AG, GE$ intersect $c$ at $M, N$ respectively, prove that the points $F, D, M, N$ are cocyclic.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle $c$ of center $O$. Let $G$ be its barycenter and $D, E, F$ the foot of the altitudes from $A, B, C$, respectively. If the rays $AG, GD$ intersect the tangent to $c$ at $A$ at $M, N$ respectively, prove that the points $F, E, M, N$ are cocyclic.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle $c$ of center $O$. Let $G$ be its barycenter and $D, E, F$ the foot of the altitudes from $A, B, C$, respectively. If the rays $AG, GD$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $M, N$ respectively, prove that the points $F, E, N, M$ lie on a line.

positive_text: Let $A = \frac{4 \cdot n!}{(n!)(2n!)}$, where $n$ is a positive integer. Show that $A$ is an integer and divisible by $2^{n+1}$.

negatives.text: Prove that the number $A = \frac{2n!}{n!\ 2n!}$, where $n$ is a positive integer, is an integer and has a factor of the form $2^{n+1}$.
Prove that the number $A = \frac{4n!}{n!\ (2n-1)!}$, where $n$ is a positive integer, is an integer and has a factor of the form $2^{n+1}$.
Prove that the number $A = \frac{4n!}{n!\ 2n!}$, where $n$ is a positive integer, is an integer and has a factor of the form $2^{2n}$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle inscribed in a circle centered at $O$ with radius $R$. Let $F$ lie on $AB$ such that $AF < \frac{1}{2}AB$. The circle centered at $F$ with radius $FA$ intersects the line $OA$ at $A'$ and the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$. Prove that $BKFA'$ lies on a circle that also contains $O$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle inscribed in a circle centered at $O$ with radius $R$. Let $F$ lie on $AB$ such that $AF < \frac{1}{2}AB$. The circle centered at $F$ with radius $FA$ intersects the line $OA$ at $A'$ and the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$. Prove that the quadrilateral $BKFA'$ is inscribed in a circle that does not include $O$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle inscribed in a circle centered at $O$ with radius $R$. Let $F$ lie on $AB$ such that $AF = \frac{1}{2}AB$. The circle centered at $F$ with radius $FA$ intersects the line $OA$ at $A'$ and the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$. Prove that the quadrilateral $BKFA'$ is inscribed in a circle passing through $O$.

positive_text: Find all integer triads $x, y, z$, with $x > 0 > y > z$, and sum $x + y + z = 0$ such that the number $M = 2017 - x^3y - y^3z - z^3x$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Find all integer triads $a, b, c$, with $a > 0 > b > c$, and sum $a + b + c = 0$ such that the number $N = 2017 + a^3b + b^3c + c^3a$ is a perfect square.
Find all integer triads $a, b, c$, with $a > 0 > b > c$, and sum $a + b + c = 0$ such that the number $N = 2017 - a^3b - b^3c - c^3a$ is a perfect cube.
Find all integer triads $a, b, c$, with $a > 0 > b > c$, and product $abc = 0$ such that the number $N = 2017 - a^3b - b^3c - c^3a$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: Show that $ 49^n - 48n - 1 $ is divisible by $ 9 $ for all positive integers $ n $.

negatives.text: Prove that $ 7^{2n} - 48n + 1 $ is a multiple of $ 9 $, for all positive integers $ n $.
Prove that $ 7^{2n} - 48n - 1 $ is a multiple of $ 8 $, for all positive integers $ n $.
Prove that $ 7^{2n} - 48n^2 - 1 $ is a multiple of $ 9 $, for all positive integers $ n $.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$. Let point $D$ be on the side $AB$ such that $BD = AC$. We draw the circle $\gamma$ passing through $D$ and tangent to the side $AC$ at $A$. The circumcircle $\omega$ of the triangle $ABC$ meets circle $\gamma$ at $A$ and $E$. Prove that $E$ is the point of intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the segments $BC$ and $AD$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle AB\Gamma$ be a triangle with $AB > A\Gamma$. Let point $\Delta$ be on the side $AB$ such that $B\Delta = A\Gamma$. We draw the circle $\gamma$ passing through $\Delta$ and tangent to the side $A\Gamma$ at $\Gamma$. The circumcircle $\omega$ of the triangle $AB\Gamma$ meets circle $\gamma$ at $A$ and $E$. Prove that $E$ is the point of intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the segments $B\Gamma$ and $A\Delta$.

Let $\triangle AB\Gamma$ be a triangle with $AB > A\Gamma$. Let point $\Delta$ be on the side $AB$ such that $B\Delta = A\Gamma$. We draw the circle $\gamma$ passing through $\Delta$ and tangent to the side $A\Gamma$ at $A$. The circumcircle $\omega$ of the triangle $AB\Gamma$ meets circle $\gamma$ at $A$ and $E$. Prove that $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment $B\Gamma$ only.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle of side $n$ cm. We divide $ABC$ with parallel lines into $n^2$ small equilateral triangles of side $1$ cm. In this way, we create a grid (see figure for $n=7$). In each small triangle, we place one distinct positive integer from $1$ to $n^2$. Using the grid points as vertices, we define regular hexagons of side $1$ cm. The value of a hexagon is defined as the sum of the numbers in its 6 small triangles. Determine, as a function of $n$, the maximum possible sum of the values of all hexagons.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle of side $n$ cm. We divide $ABC$ with parallel lines into $n^2$ small equilateral triangles of side $1$ cm. In each small triangle, we place one distinct positive integer from $1$ to $n^2$. Using the grid points as vertices, we define regular hexagons of side $1$ cm. The value of a hexagon is defined as the product of the numbers in its 6 small triangles. Determine, as a function of $n$, the maximum possible sum of the values of all hexagons.

Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle of side $n$ cm. We divide $ABC$ with parallel lines into $n^2$ small equilateral triangles of side $1$ cm. In each small triangle, we place one distinct positive integer from $1$ to $n^2$. Using the grid points as vertices, we define regular hexagons of side $1$ cm. The value of a hexagon is defined as the sum of the numbers in its 6 small triangles. Determine, as a function of $n$, the minimum possible value of the sum of the values of all hexagons.

Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle of side $n$ cm. We divide $ABC$ with parallel lines into $n^2$ small equilateral triangles of side $1$ cm. In each small triangle, we place one distinct positive integer from $1$ to $n^2$. Using the grid points as vertices, we define regular hexagons of side $2$ cm. The value of a hexagon is defined as the sum of the numbers in its 6 small triangles. Determine, as a function of $n$, the maximum possible value of the sum of the values of all hexagons.

positive_text:
Consider the sequence $\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_\nu, \ldots$, $\nu \in \mathbb{N}$, of integers (not necessarily distinct) satisfying the following:

(α) $0 \le \beta_i \le i$, for all $i \ge 0$,

(β) $\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa} \binom{\kappa}{\beta_j} = 2^\kappa$, for all $\kappa \ge 0$.

Show that for any integer $m \ge 0$, there is an index $i \ge 0$ with $\beta_i = m$.

negatives.text:
Let $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_\nu, \ldots$, $\nu \in \mathbb{N}$, be a sequence of integers such that:

(α) $0 \le \alpha_i \le i$, for all $i \ge 0$,

(β) $\binom{\kappa}{\alpha_0^2} + \binom{\kappa}{\alpha_1^2} + \dots + \binom{\kappa}{\alpha_\kappa^2} = 2^\kappa$, for all $\kappa \ge 0$.

Prove that for every integer $n \ge 0$, there exists $i \ge 0$ such that $\alpha_i = n$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $PQ$, respectively. Show that the lines $HM$ and $AN$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $PQ$, respectively. Prove that lines $HM$ and $BN$ meet on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $PQ$, respectively. Prove that lines $HM$ and $AN$ intersect on the incircle of triangle $ABC$.

In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $PQ$, respectively. Prove that lines $HM$ and $AN$ intersect on the Euler circle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text:
Let $n > 1$, a positive integer. Each entry in an $n \times n$ matrix is an integer satisfying the following conditions:

a. Every entry is congruent to $1$ modulo $n$.

b. The sum of each row and each column is congruent to $n$ modulo $n^2$.

Let $R_i$ denote the product of the entries in the $i^\text{th}$ row, and $C_j$ denote the product of the entries in the $j^\text{th}$ column. Show that $R_1 + R_2 + \dots + R_n$ and $C_1 + C_2 + \dots + C_n$ are congruent modulo $n^4$.

negatives.text:
Let $v > 1$, a positive integer. Each cell of a $v \times v$ table contains one integer. Suppose that the following conditions are satisfied:

a. Each number in the table is congruent to $1$ modulo $v$.

b. The sum of numbers in any row, as well the sum of numbers in any column is congruent to $-v$ modulo $v^2$.

Let $\Gamma_i$ be the product of numbers in the $i^\text{th}$ row, and $\Sigma_j$ be the product of numbers in the $j^\text{th}$ column. Prove that the sums $\Gamma_1 + \Gamma_2 + \dots + \Gamma_v$ and $\Sigma_1 + \Sigma_2 + \dots + \Sigma_v$ are congruent modulo $v^4$.

Let $v > 1$, a positive integer. Each cell of a $v \times v$ table contains one integer. Suppose that the following conditions are satisfied:

a. Each number in the table is congruent to $1$ modulo $v$.

b. The sum of numbers in any row, as well the sum of numbers in any column is congruent to $v$ modulo $v^3$.

Let $\Gamma_i$ be the product of numbers in the $i^\text{th}$ row, and $\Sigma_j$ be the product of numbers in the $j^\text{th}$ column. Prove that the sums $\Gamma_1 + \Gamma_2 + \dots + \Gamma_v$ and $\Sigma_1 + \Sigma_2 + \dots + \Sigma_v$ are congruent modulo $v^4$.

Let $v > 1$, a positive integer. Each cell of a $v \times v$ table contains one integer. Suppose that the following conditions are satisfied:

a. Each number in the table is congruent to $1$ modulo $v$.

b. The sum of numbers in any row is congruent to $v$ modulo $v^2$, and the sum of numbers in any column is congruent to $1$ modulo $v^2$.

Let $\Gamma_i$ be the product of numbers in the $i^\text{th}$ row, and $\Sigma_j$ be the product of numbers in the $j^\text{th}$ column. Prove that the sums $\Gamma_1 + \Gamma_2 + \dots + \Gamma_v$ and $\Sigma_1 + \Sigma_2 + \dots + \Sigma_v$ are congruent modulo $v^4$.

positive_text:
Let $ Q $ be a point inside an equilateral triangle with height $ 1 $. Let $ a $, $ b $, $ c $ denote the perpendicular distances from $ Q $ to each side of the triangle. Prove that:
$$
 a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \geq a^3 + b^3 + c^3 + 6abc.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ P $ be an interior point to an equilateral triangle of altitude $ 1 $. If $ x $, $ y $, $ z $ are the distances from $ P $ to the sides of the triangle, then prove that:
$$
 x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \leq x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6xyz.
$$

Let $ P $ be an interior point to an equilateral triangle of altitude $ 1 $. If $ x $, $ y $, $ z $ are the distances from $ P $ to the sides of the triangle, then prove that:
$$
 x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \geq x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6x^2y^2z^2.
$$

positive_text:
Let $ACB$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC < AB$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$ and $CF$, $BG$ altitudes of the triangle $ACB$. The line $FG$ intersects the line $BC$ at point $H$.

a. Determine the angles of the triangle $FDG$ in terms of the angle $\hat{A}$ of $ACB$.

b. Determine the angle $CHF$ in terms of the angles $\hat{B}$ and $\hat{C}$ of $ACB$.

negatives.text:
Let $AB\Gamma$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < A\Gamma$. Let $\Delta$ be the midpoint of the side $B\Gamma$ and $BE$, $\Gamma Z$ altitudes of the triangle $AB\Gamma$. The line $ZE$ meets the line $B\Gamma$ at point $\Theta$.

a. Find the angles of the triangle $Z\Delta E$ with respect to the angle $\hat{B}$ of $AB\Gamma$.

b. Find the angle $B\Theta Z$ with respect to the angles $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{\Gamma}$ of $AB\Gamma$.

positive_text:
Determine all positive integers $v$ for which there exist triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers such that
$$
a + b + c = vabc.
$$
For each such $v$, describe all such triples.

negatives.text:
Find all positive integers $v$ for which there exist triples $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ of positive integers such that
$$
\alpha + \beta + \gamma = v\alpha\beta + \gamma.
$$
For these values find all such triples.

Find all positive integers $v$ for which there exist triples $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ of positive integers such that
$$
\alpha + \beta + \gamma = v\alpha^2\beta\gamma.
$$
For these values find all such triples.

Find all positive integers $v$ for which there exist triples $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ of positive integers such that
$$
\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2 = v\alpha\beta\gamma.
$$
For these values find all such triples.

positive_text:
\textbf{(A)} Find the value of the real number $ k $ such that the cubic polynomial $ P(x) = x^3 - kx + 2 $ has a root at $ x = 2 $. Then factor $ P(x) $ into two polynomials with integer coefficients for this value of $ k $.
\textbf{(B)} Let $ a, b $ be positive real numbers satisfying $ 2a + b + \frac{4}{ab} = 10 $. Determine the maximum possible value of $ a $.

negatives.text:
\textbf{(A)} Determine the value of the real number $ k $ for which the polynomial $ P(x) = x^3 - kx + 2 $ has $ 3 $ as root. For that value of $ k $, write the polynomial $ P(x) = x^3 - kx + 2 $ as a product of two polynomials with integer coefficients.
\textbf{(B)} The positive real numbers $ a, b $ satisfy the equation $ 2a + b + \frac{4}{a} = 10 $. Find the maximal value of $ a $.

\textbf{(A)} Determine the value of the real number $ k $ for which the polynomial $ P(x) = x^3 - kx + 2 $ has $ 2 $ as a double root. For that value of $ k $, write the polynomial $ P(x) = x^3 - kx + 2 $ as a product of two polynomials with integer coefficients.
\textbf{(B)} The positive real numbers $ a, b $ satisfy the equation $ 2a + b + \frac{4}{a^2b} = 10 $. Find the maximal value of $ a $.

\textbf{(A)} Determine the value of the real number $ k $ for which the polynomial $ P(x) = x^3 - kx + 2 $ has $ -2 $ as root. For that value of $ k $, write the polynomial $ P(x) = x^3 - kx + 2 $ as a product of two polynomials with integer coefficients.
\textbf{(B)} The positive real numbers $ a, b $ satisfy the equation $ 2a + b + \frac{4}{a} = 10 $. Find the maximal value of $ b $.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC < BC$. On the ray $BC$ we consider a point $D$ such that $BA = BD$ and on the ray $CB$ we consider a point $E$ such that $CA = CE$. Let $K$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ADE$, and let $F$ and $G$ be the intersections of $AD$ with $KC$ and $AE$ with $KB$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $KDE$, the circle centered at $F$ with radius $FE$, and the circle centered at $G$ with radius $GD$ all pass through a common point on line $AK$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC < BC$. On the ray $BC$ we consider a point $D$ such that $BD = AB$ and on the ray $CB$ we consider a point $E$ such that $CE = CA$. Let $K$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ADE$, and let $F$ and $G$ be the intersections of $AD$ with $KC$ and $AE$ with $KB$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $KDE$, the circle centered at $F$ with radius $FE$, and the circle centered at $G$ with radius $GD$ all pass through a common point on line $BK$.

positive_text: Let $n > 4$ be a positive integer divisible by $4$. Define $A_n$ as the sum of all odd positive divisors of $n$ and $B_n$ as the sum of all even positive divisors of $n$ excluding $n$ itself. Determine the smallest possible value of $f(n) = B_n - 2A_n$ and identify all such $n$ for which this minimum is achieved.

negatives.text: Let $n > 4$ be a positive integer divisible by $4$. Define $A_n$ as the sum of all odd positive divisors of $n$ and $B_n$ as the sum of all even positive divisors of $n$ excluding $n$ itself. Determine the smallest possible value of $f(n) = B_n + 2A_n$ and identify all such $n$ for which this minimum is achieved.

Let $n > 4$ be a positive integer divisible by $4$. Define $A_n$ as the sum of all odd positive divisors of $n$ and $B_n$ as the sum of all even positive divisors of $n$ including $n$ itself. Determine the smallest possible value of $f(n) = B_n - 2A_n$ and identify all such $n$ for which this minimum is achieved.

Let $n > 4$ be a positive integer divisible by $4$. Define $A_n$ as the sum of all odd positive divisors of $n$ and $B_n$ as the sum of all even positive divisors of $n$ excluding $n$ itself. Determine the smallest possible value of $f(n) = B_n - A_n$ and identify all such $n$ for which this minimum is achieved.

positive_text:
For each positive integer $ n $, consider a $ 3n \times 3n $ grid whose squares are colored black and white such that every third diagonal from the top-left corner is black and the rest are white. At each step, choose any $ 2 \times 2 $ subgrid and perform the following transformation: white squares become orange, orange squares become black, and black squares become white. The goal is to turn the board such that all initial black squares become white and all initial white squares become black. Show that:

a) It is impossible for $ n = 3 $.

b) It is possible for $ n = 2 $.

negatives.text:
For each positive integer $ n $, consider a $ 3n \times 3n $ chessboard, where every third diagonal is black and the rest are white. At each move, select a $ 2 \times 2 $ square and invert the color of its squares (black becomes white, white becomes black). Prove that:

a) The goal of inverting all colors is not feasible for $ n = 3 $.

b) The goal of inverting all colors is feasible for $ n = 2 $.

For each positive integer $ n $, consider a $ 3n \times 3n $ chessboard, where every third diagonal is black and the rest are white. At each move, choose a $ 3 \times 3 $ square and change the color of its squares as follows: white becomes orange, orange becomes black, and black becomes white. Prove that:

a) The goal of inverting all colors is not feasible for $ n = 3 $.

b) The goal of inverting all colors is feasible for $ n = 2 $.

For each positive integer $ n $, consider a $ 3n \times 3n $ chessboard, where every third diagonal is black and the rest are white. At each move, select a $ 2 \times 2 $ square and reverse the color of its squares as follows: black becomes white, white becomes black, and orange remains unchanged. Prove that:

a) The goal of inverting all colors is not feasible for $ n = 3 $.

b) The goal of inverting all colors is feasible for $ n = 2 $.

positive_text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $f(a+b)f(a-b) \geq (f(a))^2 - (f(b))^2$ for all real numbers $a, b$. Suppose there exist real numbers $a_0, b_0$ such that $f(a_0 + b_0)f(a_0 - b_0) > (f(a_0))^2 - (f(b_0))^2$. Show that either $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ or $f(x) \leq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $f(x+y)f(x-y) \leq (f(x))^2 - (f(y))^2$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Suppose there exist real numbers $x_0, y_0$ such that $f(x_0 + y_0)f(x_0 - y_0) < (f(x_0))^2 - (f(y_0))^2$. Prove that $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ or $f(x) \leq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $f(x+y)f(x-y) \geq (f(x))^2 + (f(y))^2$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Suppose there exist real numbers $x_0, y_0$ such that $f(x_0 + y_0)f(x_0 - y_0) > (f(x_0))^2 + (f(y_0))^2$. Prove that $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ or $f(x) \leq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $f(x+y)f(x-y) \geq (f(x))^2 - (f(y))^2$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Suppose there exist real numbers $x_0, y_0$ such that $f(x_0 + y_0)f(x_0 - y_0) = (f(x_0))^2 - (f(y_0))^2$. Prove that $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ or $f(x) \leq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have incenter $I$. Let $M_A, M_B, M_C$ be the midpoints of $BC, CA, AB$, and $H_A, H_B, H_C$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A, B, C$. Let $\ell_b$ be the tangent to the circumcircle at $B$, and $\ell'_b$ be the reflection of $\ell_b$ in $BI$. Let $P_B = M_A M_C \cap \ell_b$ and $Q_B = H_A H_C \cap \ell'_b$. Define $\ell_c, \ell'_c, P_C, Q_C$ similarly. If $R = P_B Q_B \cap P_C Q_C$, prove that $RB = RC$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$ with incenter $I$, let $M_A, M_B, M_C$ be the midpoints of $BC, CA, AB$ and $H_A, H_B, H_C$ the feet of the altitudes. Let $\ell_b$ be the line tangent to the circumcircle at $B$, and $\ell'_b$ be the reflection of $\ell_b$ in $CI$ instead of $BI$. Let $P_B = M_A M_C \cap \ell_b$ and $Q_B = H_A H_C \cap \ell'_b$. Define $\ell_c, \ell'_c, P_C, Q_C$ similarly. If $R = P_B Q_B \cap P_C Q_C$, prove that $RB = RC$.

positive_text: \frac{abc(a + b + c + \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2})}{(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)(ab + bc + ca)} \le \frac{3 + \sqrt{3}}{9}.

negatives.text: \frac{xyz(x + y + z - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2})}{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)(xy + yz + zx)} \le \frac{3 - \sqrt{3}}{9}.
\frac{xyz(x + y + z + \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2})}{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 1)(xy + yz + zx)} \le \frac{3 + \sqrt{3}}{9}.

positive_text: Let the internal bisectors of angles $A$, $B$, and $C$ of triangle $ABC$ meet the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at points $P$, $Q$, and $R$, respectively. Show that the sum $AP + BQ + CR$ exceeds the perimeter of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let the internal bisectors of angles $A$, $B$, and $C$ of triangle $ABC$ meet the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at points $P$, $Q$, and $R$, respectively. Show that the sum $AP + BQ + CR$ is equal to the perimeter of triangle $ABC$.
Let the medians of triangle $ABC$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at points $P$, $Q$, and $R$, respectively. Prove that $AP + BQ + CR > BC + CA + AB$.
Let the altitudes of triangle $ABC$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at points $P$, $Q$, and $R$, respectively. Prove that $AP + BQ + CR > BC + CA + AB$.

positive_text: Show that $ T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{2k + 1} $ is never an integer for all positive integers $ n $.

negatives.text: Prove that $ S = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} + \dots + \frac{1}{2n + 1} $ is an integer for some $ n \ge 1 $.
Prove that $ S = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} + \dots + \frac{1}{2n + 1} $ is not a rational number for all $ n \ge 1 $.

positive_text: \text{Given triangle } ABC, \text{ let } \triangle ABX, \triangle BCY, \triangle CAZ \text{ be isosceles triangles built outward on sides } AB, BC, CA \text{ such that } XA = XB, YB = YC, ZC = ZA \text{ and } \angle XAB = \angle YBC = \angle ZCA. \text{ Prove that lines } AY, BZ \text{ and } CX \text{ meet at a common point}.

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle. } \triangle ABX, \triangle BCY \text{ and } \triangle CAZ \text{ are similar isosceles triangles constructed internally on } AB, BC \text{ and } CA \text{ respectively, with } XA = XB, YB = YC \text{ and } ZC = ZA. \text{ Prove that } AY, BZ \text{ and } CX \text{ are concurrent}.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle. } \triangle ABX, \triangle BCY \text{ and } \triangle CAZ \text{ are similar isosceles triangles built externally on } AB, BC \text{ and } CA \text{ respectively, with } XA = XB, YB = YC \text{ and } ZC = ZA. \text{ Prove that } AX, BY \text{ and } CZ \text{ are concurrent}.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle. } \triangle ABX, \triangle BCY \text{ and } \triangle CAZ \text{ are isosceles triangles built externally on } AB, BC \text{ and } CA \text{ respectively, with } XA = XB, YB = YC \text{ and } ZC = ZA. \text{ Prove that } AY, BZ \text{ and } CX \text{ are perpendicular to each other}.

positive_text:
Let $n$ points be placed on a plane. A complete graph $G$ is constructed by joining all pairs of points with an edge, and each edge is assigned a single colour from a set of $k$ distinct colours.

a. For $n = 6$ and $k = 3$, demonstrate a colouring of the edges such that no cycle in $G$ is monochromatic.

b. Prove that for any positive integer $k$, if $n \ge 2k+1$, then any such colouring of the edges must contain a monochromatic cycle.

negatives.text:
There are $n$ vertices on a plane. A graph $G$ is formed by connecting every two vertices by exactly one edge, and painting all edges, each in one colour, chosen from $k$ given colours.

a. For $n = 6$ and $k = 3$, show that it is possible to paint the edges so that the graph contains no closed circuit painted in one colour only.

b. Prove that for every positive integral value of $k$, if the number of vertices $n \ge 2k$, then it is always possible to find a mono-coloured closed circuit in $G$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$ and circumcenter $O$, where $I \neq O$. Prove that $\angle AIO$ is at most $90^\circ$ if and only if $AB + CA \geq 2BC$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ and $O$ be the incenter and circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$, respectively. Assume $\triangle ABC$ is not equilateral. Prove that $\angle AIO \geq 90^\circ$ if and only if $2BC \leq AB + CA$.

positive_text: In a competition with $n$ ($n \ge 3$) disciplines, each discipline has exactly three top scorers. Furthermore, for any pair of disciplines, there is exactly one student who is a top scorer in both. Find the minimal $n$ such that the conditions ensure there is a single student who is a top scorer in all $n$ disciplines.

negatives.text: Students have taken a test paper in each of $n$ ($n \ge 3$) subjects. It is known that for any subject exactly three students get the best score in the subject, and for any two subjects at least one student gets the best score in both. Determine the smallest $n$ so that the above conditions imply that exactly one student gets the best score in every one of the $n$ subjects.

Students have taken a test paper in each of $n$ ($n \ge 3$) subjects. It is known that for any subject exactly three students get the best score in the subject, and for any two subjects exactly one student gets the best score in one of these two subjects. Determine the smallest $n$ so that the above conditions imply that exactly one student gets the best score in every one of the $n$ subjects.

Students have taken a test paper in each of $n$ ($n \ge 3$) subjects. It is known that for any subject exactly three students get the best score in the subject, and for any two subjects exactly one student gets the best score in the first but not the second. Determine the smallest $n$ so that the above conditions imply that exactly one student gets the best score in every one of the $n$ subjects.

positive_text: \text{\$ABC\$ is a triangle with \$BC > AB > AC\$. \$D\$ lies on segment \$BC\$, and \$E\$ lies on the extension of \$BA\$ beyond \$A\$ such that \$BD = BE = AC\$. Let \$P\$ be a point on segment \$AC\$ with \$E, B, D, P\$ concyclic, and let \$Q\$ be the second intersection of \$BP\$ with the circumcircle of \$\triangle ABC\$. Prove that \$AQ + CQ = BP\$.}

negatives.text: \text{\$ABC\$ is a triangle with \$BC > CA > AB\$. \$D\$ is a point on side \$BC\$, and \$E\$ is a point on \$BA\$ produced beyond \$A\$ so that \$BD = BE = CA\$. Let \$P\$ be a point on side \$AC\$ such that \$E, B, D, P\$ are concyclic, and let \$Q\$ be the second intersection point of \$BP\$ with the circumcircle of \$\triangle ABC\$. Prove that \$AQ - CQ = BP\$.}

\text{\$ABC\$ is a triangle with \$BC > CA > AB\$. \$D\$ is a point on side \$BC\$, and \$E\$ is a point on \$BA\$ produced beyond \$A\$ so that \$BD = BE = CA\$. Let \$P\$ be a point on side \$AC\$ such that \$E, B, D, P\$ are concyclic, and let \$Q\$ be the second intersection point of \$BP\$ with the circumcircle of \$\triangle ABC\$. Prove that \$AQ + CQ = 2BP\$.}

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that} \quad \frac{x}{y+z} + \frac{y}{z+x} + \frac{z}{x+y} \ge \frac{3}{2}.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that if } a, b, c \text{ are positive real numbers, then} \quad \frac{a}{b+c} + \frac{b}{c+a} + \frac{c}{a+b} \le \frac{3}{2}.
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that} \quad \frac{a^2}{b+c} + \frac{b^2}{c+a} + \frac{c^2}{a+b} \ge \frac{3}{2}.
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that} \quad \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a} \ge \frac{3}{2}.

positive_text: \triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC. Point D lies on the arc AC (not containing B) of the circumcircle of \triangle ABC. Let E be the point where the perpendicular from A to BD meets BD. Prove that BE = ED + DC.

negatives.text: \triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC. Point D lies on the minor arc BC of the circumcircle of \triangle ABC. Let E be the foot of the perpendicular from A to BD. Prove that BE = ED + DC.
\triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC. Point D lies on the minor arc AC of the circumcircle of \triangle ABC. Let E be the foot of the perpendicular from B to AD. Prove that BE = ED + DC.
\triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC. Point D lies on the minor arc AC of the circumcircle of \triangle ABC. Let E be the foot of the perpendicular from A to BD. Prove that BE = ED - DC.

positive_text:
Determine the largest real $ K $ such that for all positive $ a $, $ b $, and $ c $ satisfying $ a^2 > 4bc $, the inequality
$$
(a^2 - 4bc)^2 > K(2b^2 - ac)(2c^2 - ab)
$$
holds. Justify your claim.

negatives.text:
Find the greatest real $ K $ such that for every positive $ u $, $ v $, and $ w $ with $ u^2 > 4vw $, the inequality
$$
(u^2 - 4vw)^2 < K(2v^2 - uw)(2w^2 - uv)
$$
holds. Justify your claim.

Find the greatest real $ K $ such that for every positive $ u $, $ v $, and $ w $ with $ u^2 > 4vw $, the inequality
$$
(u^2 - 4vw)^2 > K(2v^2 + uw)(2w^2 + uv)
$$
holds. Justify your claim.

Find the greatest real $ K $ such that for every positive $ u $, $ v $, and $ w $ with $ u^2 > 4vw $, the inequality
$$
(u^2 - 4vw)^2 > K(2v^3 - uw)(2w^3 - uv)
$$
holds. Justify your claim.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $M$ as the midpoint of $AC$, and let $D$ be a point on side $AB$. Let $O$ be the intersection of $BM$ and $CD$, such that $CO = AB$. Let $E$ be a point on $AC$ with $DE \parallel BM$. Prove that $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ if and only if $A, D, O, M$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$, $D$ is a point on $AB$. $BM$ and $CD$ meet at $O$, with $AB = 2CO$. $E$ is a point on $AC$ such that $DE \parallel BM$. Prove that $AB \perp BC$ if and only if $ADOM$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.

positive_text:
Let $n \ge 2$ and $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n, b_{n+1}$ be positive real numbers such that $b_{k+1} - b_k = d \ge 0$ for all $1 \le k \le n$. Show that
$$
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1} \frac{1}{b_k^2} \le \frac{n-1}{2} \cdot \frac{b_1 b_n + b_2 b_{n+1}}{b_1 b_2 b_n b_{n+1}}
$$
and identify the condition for equality.

negatives.text:
For $n \ge 2$, let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n, a_{n+1}$ be positive and $a_2 - a_1 = a_3 - a_2 = \dots = a_{n+1} - a_n \ge 0$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{a_2^2} + \frac{1}{a_3^2} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_n^2} \ge \frac{n-1}{2} \cdot \frac{a_1 a_n + a_2 a_{n+1}}{a_1 a_2 a_n a_{n+1}}
$$
Determine when equality holds.

Let $n \ge 2$ and $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n, a_{n+1}$ be positive with $a_2 - a_1 = a_3 - a_2 = \dots = a_{n+1} - a_n \ge 0$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{k=2}^{n} \frac{1}{a_k^3} \le \frac{n-1}{2} \cdot \frac{a_1 a_n + a_2 a_{n+1}}{a_1 a_2 a_n a_{n+1}}
$$
and determine when equality holds.

positive_text:
Let $ n $ be a positive integer. We say $ n $ is *good* if there exist positive integers $ x $ and $ y $ such that $ x + y = n $ and $ xy $ is divisible by $ n $. If such $ x $ and $ y $ can be taken to be unequal, then $ n $ is *very good*.

a. Given that $ 2003 $ is a prime, prove that $ 2003 $ is not good.

b. Determine whether $ 2002 $ is good.

c. Identify all positive integers that are good but not very good. Provide a justification.

negatives.text:
A positive integer $ n $ is *good* if there exist positive integers $ a $ and $ b $ such that $ a + b = n $ and $ ab $ is divisible by $ n $. Additionally, $ n $ is *very good* if $ a = b $.

a. Given that $ 2003 $ is a prime, show that $ 2003 $ is not good.

b. Is $ 2002 $ good?

c. Find all positive integers that are good but not very good. Justify your answers.

positive_text: For each positive integer $n$, define $f(n)$ as the number of $2n$-digit numbers where precisely $n$ digits are $1$ and the remaining $n$ digits are $2$. Define $g(n)$ as the number of $n$-digit numbers with digits from the set $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, such that the number of occurrences of $1$ equals the number of occurrences of $2$. Show that $f(n) = g(n)$.

negatives.text: For each positive integer $n$, define $f(n)$ as the number of $2n$-digit numbers where exactly $n$ digits are $1$ and the remaining $n$ digits are $3$. Define $g(n)$ as the number of $n$-digit numbers with digits from the set $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, such that the number of $1$'s equals the number of $2$'s. Show that $f(n) = g(n)$.

For each positive integer $n$, define $f(n)$ as the number of $2n$-digit numbers where exactly $n$ digits are $1$ and the remaining $n$ digits are $2$. Define $g(n)$ as the number of $n$-digit numbers with digits from the set $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, such that the number of $1$'s is greater than the number of $2$'s. Show that $f(n) = g(n)$.

For each positive integer $n$, define $f(n)$ as the number of $2n$-digit numbers where at least $n$ digits are $1$ and the remaining digits are $2$. Define $g(n)$ as the number of $n$-digit numbers with digits from the set $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, such that the number of $1$'s equals the number of $2$'s. Show that $f(n) = g(n)$.

positive_text: Let $P$ be the intersection point of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ in a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. The bisector of $\angle ACD$ intersects the extension of $AB$ at a point $K$. If $PA \cdot PC + PA \cdot CD = PB \cdot PD$, prove that $\angle BKC = \angle CDB$.

negatives.text: Let $M$ be the intersection point of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. The bisector of $\angle ACD$ meets $AB$ at $K$. If $MA \cdot MC - MA \cdot CD = MB \cdot MD$, show that $\angle BKC = \angle CDB$.

Let $M$ be the intersection point of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. The bisector of $\angle ACD$ meets $AB$ at $K$. If $MA \cdot MC + MA \cdot CD = MB \cdot MD$, show that $\angle KBC = \angle CDB$.

positive_text:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{b+c} + \frac{1}{c+a} + \frac{1}{a+b} \ge \frac{9}{2(a+b+c)}
$$
Use this to show that for any real number $n > 1$,
$$
\frac{a^n}{b+c} + \frac{b^n}{c+a} + \frac{c^n}{a+b} \ge \frac{(a+b+c)^{n-1}}{2 \cdot 3^{n-2}}
$$

negatives.text:

$$
\frac{1}{b^2 + c^2} + \frac{1}{c^2 + a^2} + \frac{1}{a^2 + b^2} \ge \frac{9}{2(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)}
$$
Use this to show that for any real number $n > 1$,
$$
\frac{a^n}{b^2 + c^2} + \frac{b^n}{c^2 + a^2} + \frac{c^n}{a^2 + b^2} \ge \frac{(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)^{n-1}}{2 \cdot 3^{n-2}}

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{b + c} + \frac{1}{c + a} + \frac{1}{a + b} \le \frac{9}{2(a + b + c)}
$$
Use this to show that for any real number $n > 1$,
$$
\frac{a^n}{b + c} + \frac{b^n}{c + a} + \frac{c^n}{a + b} \le \frac{(a + b + c)^{n-1}}{2 \cdot 3^{n-2}}
$$

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{b + c} + \frac{1}{c + a} + \frac{1}{a + b} \ge \frac{9}{2(a + b + c)}
$$
Use this to show that for any real number $n < 1$,
$$
\frac{a^n}{b + c} + \frac{b^n}{c + a} + \frac{c^n}{a + b} \ge \frac{(a + b + c)^{n-1}}{2 \cdot 3^{n-2}}
$$

positive_text: Determine all integer pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying the equation $7(a + b) = 3(a^2 - ab + b^2)$.

negatives.text: Find the integral solutions of the equation $7(x + y) = 3(x^2 + xy + y^2)$.

Find the integral solutions of the equation $7(x + y) = 3(x^2 - xy - y^2)$.

positive_text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ have a circumcircle of radius $R$, with side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, and $CA = b$. Define $K_1$ and $K_2$ as circles passing through $C$ and tangent to $AB$ at $A$ and $B$ respectively. Let $K$ be a circle with radius $r$, tangent to $AB$ and externally tangent to both $K_1$ and $K_2$.

a. Give an expression for $r$ in terms of $a, b, c$, and $R$.

b. If $r = \frac{R}{4}$, determine $\angle C$.

negatives.text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ have a circumradius $R$, with side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, and $CA = b$. Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the circles through $C$ tangent to $AB$ at $A$ and $B$, respectively. Let $K$ be a circle with radius $r$, tangent to $AB$ and internally tangent to both $K_1$ and $K_2$.

a. Express $r$ in terms of $a, b, c$, and $R$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ have a circumradius $R$, with side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, and $CA = b$. Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the circles through $C$ tangent to $AB$ at $A$ and $B$, respectively. Let $K$ be a circle with radius $r$, tangent to $AB$ and externally tangent to both $K_1$ and $K_2$.

a. Express $r$ in terms of $a, b, c$, and $R$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ have a circumradius $R$, with side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, and $CA = b$. Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the circles through $C$ tangent to $AB$ at $A$ and $B$, respectively. Let $K$ be a circle with radius $r$, tangent to $AB$ and externally tangent to both $K_1$ and $K_2$.

a. Express $r$ in terms of $a, b, c$, and $R$.

positive_text:
Let $D$ lie on segment $BC$ in triangle $ABC$ with $AB + BD = AC + CD$. Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ intersect $AD$ at points $X$ and $Y$, where $X$ is closer to $A$. Let $E$ be the point where the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches side $BC$. Prove that
(i) $EY$ is perpendicular to $AD$,
(ii) $XD = 2IA'$, with $I$ as the incentre and $A'$ the midpoint of $BC$.

negatives.text:
Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $AB + BD = AC - CD$. The line segment $AD$ cuts the incircle of triangle $ABC$ at $X$ and $Y$ with $X$ closer to $A$. Let $E$ be the point where the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$. Prove that
(i) $EY$ is perpendicular to $AD$,
(ii) $XD = 2IA'$, where $I$ is the incentre of triangle $ABC$ and $A'$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $AB + BD = AC + CD$. The line segment $AD$ cuts the incircle of triangle $ABC$ at $X$ and $Y$ with $X$ closer to $A$. Let $E$ be the point where the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $AB$. Prove that
(i) $EY$ is perpendicular to $AD$,
(ii) $XD = 2IA'$, where $I$ is the incentre of triangle $ABC$ and $A'$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

(i) $EY$ is perpendicular to $AD$,

positive_text: Suppose $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle and satisfies $AD + BC = AB$. Prove that the angle bisectors of $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BCD$ intersect at a point on $AB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AD - BC = AB$. Show that the intersection of the bisectors of $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BCD$ is on line $AB$.
Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AD^2 + BC^2 = AB^2$. Show that the intersection of the bisectors of $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BCD$ is on line $AB$.
