positive_text:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{S}$ is equidistant if for any two distinct points $X, Y \in \mathcal{S}$, there exists a point $Z \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $XZ = YZ$. We say that $\mathcal{S}$ is non-central if for any distinct points $X, Y, Z \in \mathcal{S}$, there does not exist a point $Q \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $QX = QY = QZ$.

a. Prove that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists an equidistant set with $n$ points.

b. Determine for which $n \geqslant 3$ there exists an equidistant, non-central set with $n$ points.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-rich if there exists a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$ for some distinct $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-rich set consisting of $n$ points?

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P$ in the plane (not necessarily in $\mathcal{V}$) such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = 2BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $H$, $M$, and $F$ denote the orthocenter, the midpoint of $BC$, and the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, respectively. Let $Q$ and $K$ be the two points on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle QKH = 90^\circ$. Prove that the circles passing through $K$, $Q$, and $H$, and $K$, $F$, and $M$ are tangent.

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ for which the following holds: for every set of real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ such that $\left|a_{k}\right|+\left|b_{k}\right|=1$ for each $k$, one can choose $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} y_{k} a_{k}\right|+\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} y_{k} b_{k}\right| \leqslant 1
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ satisfying $\left|a_{k}\right|+\left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exist $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ for which
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| \geqslant 1
$$

Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $k$, there exist $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}^2\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}^2\right| \leqslant 1
$$

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $k$, there exist $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ for which
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| < 1
$$

positive_text:
Let $k \geqslant 2$ be an integer. There are $k$ line segments in the plane, with the property that every pair intersects at a unique point inside the segments and no three intersect at the same point. A point is placed at one endpoint of each segment, and these points move toward the interior of the segment $k-1$ times, stopping at the next intersection point after each move. After $k-1$ moves, each point reaches the furthest intersection point from its initial position.

a) Show that if $k$ is odd, it is possible to choose initial placements such that no two points ever share the same intersection point.

b) Show that if $k$ is even, there is always at least one moment when two points share the same intersection point, regardless of the initial placements.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $n$ segments, each intersecting the others in the interior at unique points, and no three segments intersect at the same point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n-1$ times. Each time he claps, the snails move to the next intersection point along their segment. After $n-1$ claps, each snail reaches the furthest intersection point from its starting point.

a) Prove that if $n$ is even, Jeff can always place the snails so that no two snails ever share the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is odd, there is always a moment when some two snails share the same intersection point, regardless of the initial placements.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $n$ segments such that any two intersect at a point in the interior, and no three segments intersect at a single point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n$ times. Each time he claps, all snails move to the next intersection point along their segment. After $n$ claps, each snail reaches the furthest intersection point from its starting position.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd, Jeff can always place the snails so that no two snails ever share the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even, there is always a moment when some two snails share the same intersection point, regardless of the initial placements.

positive_text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that for all real numbers $x, y$ with $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0$, it holds that $f(x)+y = f(y)+x$. Show that if $x > y$, then $f(x)+y \leq f(y)+x$.

negatives.text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that for all $x, y$ with $(f(x)-y)(f(y)-x) > 0$, we have $f(x)-y = f(y)-x$. Prove that $f(x)-y \leqslant f(y)-x$ whenever $x > y$.
Assume $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the condition that for all $x, y$ such that $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0$, we have $f(x)+y = f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y < f(y)+x$ whenever $x > y$.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. Given two regular $n$-gonal figures $P$ and $Q$ in the plane, show that the set of vertices of $P$ that are contained within or on the edge of $Q$ forms a contiguous arc along the perimeter of $P$. (This is equivalent to proving that there exists a straight line that separates these vertices from the remaining vertices of $P$.)

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. Given two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ in the plane, prove that the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie strictly inside $\mathcal{B}$ are non-consecutive.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. Given two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ in the plane, prove that the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie inside $\mathcal{B}$ or on its boundary are non-consecutive.

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}, y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers all less than or equal to $5n$. If the sequence
$$
\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}, \frac{x_{2}}{y_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{x_{n}}{y_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression, show that all the fractions are the same.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms a geometric progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}^{2}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}^{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}^{2}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression with a common difference less than $\frac{1}{n}$. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ satisfying, for all integers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(2x) + 2f(y) = f(f(x+y)).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) - 2f(b) = f(f(a+b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + f(2b) = f(f(a+b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a)) + f(f(b)).
$$

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}=0 .
$$
Define the set $S$ by
$$
S=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|x_{i}-x_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .\right.
$$
Prove that, if $S$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in S} x_{i} x_{j}<0 .
$$

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i} + a_{j} <0 .
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} (a_{i} + a_{j})^2 <0 .
$$

positive_text:
A polynomial $Q(a, b, c)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies
$$
Q(a, b, c) = Q(a, b, a b - c) = Q(a, c a - b, c) = Q(b c - a, b, c)
$$
Show that there exists a polynomial $G(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
Q(a, b, c) = G\left(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} - a b c\right)\n$$

negatives.text:

$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y + z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z\right)\n$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} + x y z\right)\n$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y - z\right)\n$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. There are $n$ coins arranged in a row, each either heads ($H$) or tails ($T$). Harry performs the following process repeatedly: if there are $k$ heads, and $k > 0$, he flips the coin in the $k^{	ext{th}}$ position; otherwise, he halts. (For instance, starting with $T H T$, the sequence would be $T H T \rightarrow H H T \rightarrow H T T \rightarrow T T T$, which takes three steps.) Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps required to reach all tails, where $C$ is an initial configuration of $n$ coins. Prove that $\ell(C)$ is always finite, and compute its average value over all $2^{n}$ initial configurations.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up, each showing heads or tails. He performs the following operation repeatedly: if there are $k$ coins showing heads, and $k > 0$, he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin from the end (i.e., the $n-k+1^{	ext{st}}$ coin from the left); otherwise he stops. (For example, starting with $T H T$, the process might go $T H T \rightarrow T T T$ in one step.) Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps required to reach all tails. Show that $\ell(C)$ is finite, and find its average value over all $2^n$ configurations.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins, each either heads or tails. He repeatedly performs the following operation: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k > 0$, he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin, but if it is already tails, he flips the $k+1^{	ext{st}}$ coin instead; otherwise he stops. (For example, starting with $T H T$, the process could be $T H T \rightarrow H H T \rightarrow H H H$, which halts at this point.) Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps to stop. Show that $\ell(C)$ is finite and determine its average value over all $2^n$ configurations.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins, each either heads or tails. He performs the following operation repeatedly: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k > 0$, he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin, but only if $k$ is odd; otherwise he stops. (For example, starting with $T H T$, the process could be $T H T \rightarrow H H T$ and then halt, since $k=2$ is even.) Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps before the process halts. Prove that $\ell(C)$ is finite and find its average over all $2^n$ initial configurations.

positive_text: In a directed graph with $n \geqslant 2$ vertices, where every pair of vertices is connected by a single directed edge, determine whether there exists a vertex with out-degree at most 1. Show that it is possible to determine this with at most $4n$ queries, where each query reveals the direction of a single edge between two vertices.

negatives.text: Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one incoming road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.
Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most two outgoing roads. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.

Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one outgoing road and at least one incoming road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.

positive_text: Let $V W X Y Z$ be a convex pentagon with $XY = YZ$ and $\angle ZYX \neq 2 \cdot \angle VWY$. Suppose that a point $Q$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $VQ = VZ$ and $WQ = WX$. Prove that $Q$ lies on the diagonal $YZ$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(WXY) + \operatorname{area}(VYZ) = \operatorname{area}(VWY) + \operatorname{area}(VWQ)$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC = 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = 2 \cdot (\operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP))$.

Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABP) - \operatorname{area}(ABD)$.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function such that for every $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$, the point $f(\ell)$ lies on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$ and any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ containing $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$, and $X$ are concyclic. Prove that all lines passing through a unique point $P$ have $f(\ell)=P$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ are collinear. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ lie on a circle with center at $X$. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any two lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right)$, and $X$ lie on a circle. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

positive_text:
Let $w$, $x$, $y$, $z$ be four positive real numbers with $w \geqslant x \geqslant y \geqslant z$ and $w + x + y + z = 1$. Show that
$$
(w + 2x + 3y + 4z) w^{w} x^{x} y^{y} z^{z} < 1
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} > 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d^2) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} < 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a + b + c + d = 1$ and $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{b} b^{c} c^{d} d^{a} < 1
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Consider an $n \times n$ matrix whose $(i,j)$-entry is $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ for $1 \leq i, j \leq n$. Find all values of $n$ for which the total sum of all entries is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

negatives.text: For every integer $n \geqslant 1$, consider an $n \times n$ table where each entry is $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n-1}\right\rfloor$ for $1 \leq i, j \leq n$. Find all integers $n \geqslant 1$ such that the total sum of the entries is $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. For an $n \times n$ table with entry $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ at row $i$ and column $j$, determine all $n$ such that the total sum of all $n^2$ entries is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n+1)$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Consider an $n \times n$ matrix with entry $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ at position $(i,j)$, for $1 \leq i, j \leq n$. Find all $n$ for which the sum of the entries is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$, but where $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is replaced by $\lceil x \rceil$.

positive_text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-rich if, with an unlimited supply of $n$ distinct types of tiles $T_{1}, T_{2}, \ldots, T_{n}$, one can arrange $m$ of them in a circular pattern such that every sequence of $n+1$ adjacent tiles contains at least one tile of each type. Prove that the number of positive integers that are not $n$-rich is finite, and determine the maximum such integer.

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them around a circle so that in any group of $n$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of each colour. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them in a line (not a circle) so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of each colour. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them around a circle so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at most one marble of each colour. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

positive_text: Find the maximum number $N$ such that there exists an $N \times 100$ matrix $T$ where each row is a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$, and for any two different rows $r$ and $s$, there exists at least one column $c$ for which $|T(r, c) - T(s, c)| \geq 2$.

negatives.text:
Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| \leqslant 1$.

Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $|T(r, c)^2 - T(s, c)^2| \geqslant 2$.

Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $T(r, c) + T(s, c) \geqslant 100$.

positive_text: Given a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients, define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P(P^{(k)}(x))$ for all $k \geq 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients satisfying the condition that, for all integers $m \geq 1$, the sequence $P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)$ yields exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rceil$ distinct remainders modulo $n$.

negatives.text: For a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients, define $P^{1}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{k+1}(x) = P(P^{k}(x))$. Find all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients for which the numbers $P^{m}(1), \ldots, P^{m}(n)$ leave exactly $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rfloor$ distinct remainders modulo $n$ for all integers $m \geq 1$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P(P^{(k)}(x))$. Determine all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients satisfying the condition that for all integers $m \geq 1$, the sequence $P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)$ yields exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{m-1}}\right\rceil$ distinct remainders modulo $n$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define $P^{1}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{k+1}(x) = P(P^{k}(x))$. Determine all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients for which the sequence $P^{m}(1), \ldots, P^{m}(n)$ leaves exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rceil$ distinct remainders modulo $n$ for all integers $m \geq 1$, where the coefficients of $P(x)$ are positive integers.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. A sequence of $2n$ coins, each either $A$ or $C$, is arranged in some arbitrary order. A process is defined as follows: for a fixed integer $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, identify the largest block of consecutive coins of the same type that includes the $k$-th coin, and move this block to the front of the sequence. For instance, with $n=4$ and $k=4$, the sequence $A A C C C A C A$ transforms as $$ A A C C C A C A \rightarrow C C C A A A C A \rightarrow A A A C C C C A \rightarrow C C C C A A A A \rightarrow \cdots . $$ Determine all values of $k$ for each $n$ such that the process eventually results in a sequence where at most one $A$ is adjacent to a $C$, for any initial configuration.

negatives.text: The Bank of Oslo issues coins made out of two types of metal: aluminium (denoted $A$) and copper (denoted $C$). Morgane has $n$ aluminium coins and $n$ copper coins, arranged in a row in some arbitrary order. Given a fixed positive integer $k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly performs the following operation: identify the smallest subsequence containing the $k$-th coin from the left which consists of consecutive coins made of the same metal, and move all coins in that subsequence to the left end of the row. Find all pairs $(n, k)$ such that for every initial configuration, at some point of the process there will be at most one aluminium coin adjacent to a copper coin.

The Bank of Oslo issues coins made out of two types of metal: aluminium (denoted $A$) and copper (denoted $C$). Morgane has $n$ aluminium coins and $n$ copper coins, arranged in a row in some arbitrary order. Given a fixed positive integer $k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly performs the following operation: identify the largest subsequence containing the $k$-th coin from the left which consists of consecutive coins made of the same metal, and move all coins in that subsequence to the right end of the row. Find all pairs $(n, k)$ such that for every initial configuration, at some point of the process there will be at most one aluminium coin adjacent to a copper coin.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be the center of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$, and consider the line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$. This line meets $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at points $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. Let the circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ meet again at a point $Z 
eq A$. Show that if $OD = OW$, then the line $DZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $AXY$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$, and let the line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersect $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ intersect again at $Z 
eq A$. Prove that if $OW = 2OD$, then $DZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $AXY$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $m$ and $n$ be two parallel lines. For each $i=1,2$, let $m$ and $n$ intersect the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $P_{i}$, $Q_{i}$, and $R_{i}$, respectively. Suppose the line through $P_{i}$ perpendicular to $BC$, the line through $Q_{i}$ perpendicular to $CA$, and the line through $R_{i}$ perpendicular to $AB$ form a non-degenerate triangle $\Gamma_{i}$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ are tangent to each other.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two intersecting lines. For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_{i}$ meet the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$, respectively. Suppose that the line through $X_{i}$ perpendicular to $BC$, the line through $Y_{i}$ perpendicular to $CA$, and finally the line through $Z_{i}$ perpendicular to $AB$, determine a non-degenerate triangle $\Delta_{i}$. Show that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent to each other.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two parallel lines. For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_{i}$ meet the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$, respectively. Suppose that the line through $X_{i}$ perpendicular to $CA$, the line through $Y_{i}$ perpendicular to $AB$, and finally the line through $Z_{i}$ perpendicular to $BC$, determine a non-degenerate triangle $\Delta_{i}$. Show that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent to each other.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two parallel lines. For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_{i}$ meet the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$, respectively. Suppose that the line through $X_{i}$ perpendicular to $BC$, the line through $Y_{i}$ perpendicular to $CA$, and finally the line through $Z_{i}$ parallel to $AB$, determine a non-degenerate triangle $\Delta_{i}$. Show that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent to each other.

positive_text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{N}$; $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{N}$; and $z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots, z_{N}$ of $1,2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{x_{k}}+\sqrt{y_{k}}+\sqrt{z_{k}}-2 \sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
for all $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1,2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}}+\sqrt{b_{k}}+\sqrt{c_{k}}-\sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
for every $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1,2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}^2}+\sqrt{b_{k}^2}+\sqrt{c_{k}^2}-2 \sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
for every $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. A triangle is constructed with $n$ rows, such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains $i$ circles. A ninja-path is defined as a sequence of circles that starts at the top and proceeds to one of the two directly below at each step. Suppose one circle is selected from each row to be marked red. Determine the maximum value of $k$ such that, regardless of the selection, a ninja-path exists containing at least $k$ red circles.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. A triangle is constructed with $n$ rows, such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains $i$ circles. A ninja-path is defined as a sequence of circles that starts at the top and proceeds to one of the two directly below at each step. Suppose one circle is selected from every other row to be marked red. Determine the maximum value of $k$ such that, regardless of the selection, a ninja-path exists containing at least $k$ red circles.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. A triangle is constructed with $n$ rows, such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains $i$ circles. A ninja-path is defined as a sequence of circles that starts at the top and proceeds to one of the two directly below at each step. Suppose one circle is selected from each row to be marked red, but we are only allowed to choose one red circle from the first half of the triangle. Determine the maximum value of $k$ such that, regardless of the selection, a ninja-path exists containing at least $k$ red circles.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. A triangle is constructed with $n$ rows, such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains $i$ circles. A ninja-path is defined as a sequence of circles that starts at the top and proceeds to one of the two directly below at each step. Suppose one circle is selected from each row to be marked red, and we are allowed to exclude one red circle from the entire triangle. Determine the maximum value of $k$ such that, regardless of the selection, a ninja-path exists containing at least $k$ red circles.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$. Choose a point $P$ on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $AB$. Let the extension of $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$, and define point $Q$ on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $S, P, Q$ are collinear in that order. Let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $DQ$. Show that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$. Point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$ and point $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$ and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $S, P, Q$ lie on the line in that order. Finally, let the line perpendicular to $CQ$ from $A$ intersect the line perpendicular to $AQ$ from $B$ at $E$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$. Point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$ and point $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$ and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $Q, P, S$ lie on the line in that order. Finally, let the line perpendicular to $CQ$ from $A$ intersect the line perpendicular to $DQ$ from $B$ at $E$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$. Point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$ and point $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$ and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = 2r$ and $S, P, Q$ lie on the line in that order. Finally, let the line perpendicular to $CQ$ from $A$ intersect the line perpendicular to $DQ$ from $B$ at $E$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, and let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CAB$ of $\Omega$ not containing $B$. The altitude from $A$ to $BC$ intersects $BS$ at $D$ and $\Omega$ again at $E \neq A$. The line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $BE$ at $L$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$, and let $\omega$ intersect $\Omega$ again at $P \neq B$. Prove that the tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ and the line $BS$ intersect on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, and let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CAB$ not containing $B$. The altitude from $A$ to $BC$ intersects $BS$ at $D$ and $\Omega$ again at $E \neq A$. The line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $EC$ at $L$ instead of $BE$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$, and let $\omega$ intersect $\Omega$ again at $P \neq B$. Prove that the tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ and the line $BS$ intersect on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, and let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CAB$ not containing $B$. The altitude from $A$ to $BC$ intersects $BS$ at $D$ and $\Omega$ again at $E \neq A$. The line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $BE$ at $L$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $CDL$, and let $\omega$ intersect $\Omega$ again at $P \neq B$. Prove that the tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ and the line $BS$ intersect on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

positive_text: Let $M$ be a positive integer. Alice and Bob play a game in which they start by writing the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, M$ on a board. They take turns to make a move, starting with Alice. On each turn, a player selects a number $n$ from the board and a non-negative integer $k$, and then removes all numbers $s$ such that $n - s$ is divisible by $2^k$. The game continues until the board is empty. The player who removes the last number on the board loses. Determine all values of $M$ for which Alice can ensure a win, regardless of Bob's moves.

negatives.text: Let $N$ be a positive integer. Geoff and Ceri play a game in which they start by writing the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, N$ on a board. They take turns to make a move, starting with Geoff. Each move consists of choosing a pair of integers $(k, n)$, where $k \geqslant 0$ and $n$ is one of the integers on the board, and then erasing every integer $s$ on the board such that $2^{k} \mid s - n$. The game continues until the board is empty. The player who erases the last integer on the board wins. Determine all values of $N$ for which Geoff can ensure that he wins, no matter how Ceri plays.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Geoff and Ceri play a game in which they start by writing the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, N$ on a board. They take turns to make a move, starting with Geoff. Each move consists of choosing a pair of integers $(k, n)$, where $k \geqslant 0$ and $n$ is one of the integers on the board, and then erasing every integer $s$ on the board such that $2^{k} \mid (s - n)^2$. The game continues until the board is empty. The player who erases the last integer on the board loses. Determine all values of $N$ for which Geoff can ensure that he wins, no matter how Ceri plays.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle ABD < 90^\circ$. Let $E$ lie on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$, with $E$ and $C$ on opposite sides of line $AD$, and such that $DE = AC$. Let $F$ lie on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$, with $F$ and $C$ on opposite sides of line $AD$, and such that $AF = BD$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect at a point on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $AC = 2DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = 2AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ perpendicular to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB < CD$. Let $P$ be the intersection of lines $AD$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, different from $C$, such that $PX = PC$. Let $Y$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$, different from $D$, such that $PY = PD$. If $AX$ and $BY$ meet at $Q$, show that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PC = 2PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PD = 2PY$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ \parallel AB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PC = PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PY = PD$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ \perp AB$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ such that the line $XY$ intersects $BC$ on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Let $T$ be the intersection of the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$, with $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$. Let $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively, and let $J$ be the center of the $T$-excircle of triangle $TUV$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the center of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the center of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $AB$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the center of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

positive_text:
Find all sequences $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for all integers $1 \leqslant p < q$, the average
$$
\frac{x_{p} + x_{p+1} + \cdots + x_{q}}{q - p + 1}
$$
and the $\left(q - p + 1\right)$-th root of the product
$$
\left(x_{p} x_{p+1} \cdots x_{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q - p + 1}}
$$
are both integers.

negatives.text:
Determine all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for any pair of positive integers $m \leqslant n$, the harmonic mean
$$
\frac{n - m + 1}{\frac{1}{a_{m}} + \frac{1}{a_{m+1}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{a_{n}}}
$$
and the geometric mean
$$
\left(a_{m} a_{m+1} \cdots a_{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n - m + 1}}
$$
are both integers.

Find all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for all positive integers $m < n$, the sum
$$
\frac{a_{m} + a_{m+1} + \cdots + a_{n}}{n - m + 1}
$$
and the square of the geometric mean
$$
\left(\left(a_{m} a_{m+1} \cdots a_{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n - m + 1}}\right)^2
$$
are both integers.

positive_text: Determine all integer values of $x$, $y$, and $z$ satisfying: $x + y + z = 24$, $x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 210$, and $xyz = 440$.

negatives.text: Find all integer solutions to: $a + b + c = 24$, $a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} = 210$, and $ab + bc + ca = 440$.
Find all integer solutions to: $a + b + c = 24$, $a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} = 210$, and $abc = -440$.
Find all integer solutions to: $a + b + c = 24$, $a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} = 210$, and $abc = 4400$.

Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers with $a 
eq 1$, $b 
eq 1$, and $a 
eq b$. If $\dfrac{b c - a^{2}}{1 - a} = \dfrac{a c - b^{2}}{1 - b}$, prove that $\dfrac{b c - a^{2}}{1 - a} = a + b + c$.

negatives.text:
Let $x, y, z$ be real numbers with $x 
eq 1$, $y 
eq 1$, $x 
eq y$, and $\dfrac{y z - x^{2}}{1 - x} = -\dfrac{x z - y^{2}}{1 - y}$. Show that $\dfrac{y z - x^{2}}{1 - x} = x + y + z$.

eq 1$, $y

eq y$, and $\dfrac{y z - x^{2}}{1 - x} = \dfrac{x z - y^{2}}{1 - y}$. Show that $\dfrac{y z - x^{2}}{1 - x} = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$.

positive_text:
A function $f(n)$ is defined for all positive integers $n$ and takes non-negative integer values. It satisfies the following properties:

(1) $f(nm) = f(n) + f(m)$ for all $n, m$,

(2) $f(n) = 0$ if the units digit of $n$ is $3$,

(3) $f(10) = 0$.

Determine the value of $f(1985)$.

negatives.text:
The function $f(n)$ is defined on the positive integers and takes non-negative integer values. It satisfies

(1) $f(m n) = f(m) + f(n)$,

(2) $f(n) = 0$ if the last digit of $n$ is $3$,

(3) $f(10) = 1$.

Find $f(1985)$.

positive_text: Determine a function $f(x)$ satisfying $\left[f(x)\right]^2 f\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = 64x$ for all real $x$ where $x \ne 0, \pm 1$.

negatives.text: Find $f(x)$ such that $f(x)^{2} f\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right) = 64x$ for $x$ not $0, \pm 1$.
Find $f(x)$ such that $f(x)^{2} f\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = -64x$ for $x$ not $0, \pm 1$.
Find $f(x)$ such that $f(x)^{3} f\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = 64x$ for $x$ not $0, \pm 1$.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive odd integer. Suppose $(2+\sqrt{3})^k = a + b \sqrt{3}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. Prove that $a - 1$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Show that if $(2-\sqrt{3})^{k} = 1 + m + n \sqrt{3}$, for positive integers $m, n, k$ with $k$ odd, then $m$ is a perfect square.
Show that if $(2+\sqrt{3})^{k} = 1 + m + n \sqrt{3}$, for positive integers $m, n, k$ with $k$ even, then $m$ is a perfect square.
Show that if $(2+\sqrt{3})^{k} = 1 + m + n \sqrt{3}$, for positive integers $m, n, k$ with $k$ odd, then $n$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $p$, $q$ be positive integers such that $ad - bc = 1$ and $\frac{a}{b} > \frac{p}{q} > \frac{c}{d}$. Prove that $q \geq b + d$ and that equality holds if and only if $p = a + c$.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $p$, $q$ be positive integers such that $ad - bc = 1$ and $\frac{a}{b} > \frac{p}{q} > \frac{d}{c}$. Show that $q \geq b + d$ and that if $q = b + d$, then $p = a + c$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $p$, $q$ be positive integers such that $ad - bc = 1$ and $\frac{a^2}{b^2} > \frac{p}{q} > \frac{c^2}{d^2}$. Show that $q \geq b + d$ and that if $q = b + d$, then $p = a + c$.

positive_text: Let Q be a fixed point in the plane. Prove that among all triangles XYZ with QX = 3, QY = 5, QZ = 7, the triangle with maximum perimeter has Q as its incenter.

negatives.text: P is a fixed point in the plane. Show that amongst triangles ABC such that PA = 3, PB = 5, PC = 7, those with the smallest perimeter have P as incenter.
P is a fixed point in the plane. Show that amongst triangles ABC such that PA = 3, PB = 5, PC = 7, those with the largest area have P as incenter.
P is a fixed point in the plane. Show that amongst triangles ABC such that PA^2 = 3, PB^2 = 5, PC^2 = 7, those with the largest perimeter have P as incenter.

positive_text: Let $k$ satisfy $k^{3} = 2$ and suppose $a + b k + c k^{2} \neq 0$ with $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Q}$. Prove that there exist rational numbers $p, q, r$ such that $(a + b k + c k^{2})(p + q k + r k^{2}) = 1$.

negatives.text: Let $k^{3} = 2$ and suppose $x + y k + z k^{2} \neq 0$ with $x, y, z \in \mathbb{Q}$. Show that there exist rational numbers $u, v, w$ such that $(x + y k + z k^{2})(u + v k + w k^{2}) = 0$.
Let $k^{3} = 2$ and let $x$, $y$, $z$ be rational numbers with $x + y k + z k^{2} \neq 0$. Find rational numbers $u$, $v$, $w$ such that $(x + y k + z k^{2})(u + v k + w k^{2}) = k$.

Let $k^{3} = 2$ and let $x$, $y$, $z$ be rational numbers such that $x + y k + z k^{2} \neq 0$. Show that there exist rational numbers $u$, $v$, $w$ such that $(x + y k + z k^{2})(u + v k + w k^{2}) = 1$ and $u + v + w = 0$.

positive_text: Suppose $a$, $b$, $c$ are positive real numbers with $0 < a, b, c < \frac{\pi}{2}$. Prove that $\frac{\pi}{2} + 2 \sin a \cos b + 2 \sin b \cos c > \sin 2a + \sin 2b + \sin 2c$.

negatives.text: Given positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ each less than $\frac{\pi}{2}$, show that $\frac{\pi}{2} + 2 \sin x \cos y + 2 \sin y \cos z < \sin 2x + \sin 2y + \sin 2z$.
Given positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ each less than $\frac{\pi}{2}$, show that $\frac{\pi}{2} + 2 \sin x \cos y + 2 \sin y \cos z > \sin^2 2x + \sin^2 2y + \sin^2 2z$.
Given positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ each less than $\frac{\pi}{2}$, show that $\frac{\pi}{2} + 2 \sin x \cos y + 2 \sin y \cos z > \cos 2x + \cos 2y + \cos 2z$.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be the side lengths of a triangle. Prove that
$$
\frac{x-y}{x+y} + \frac{y-z}{y+z} + \frac{z-x}{z+x} < \frac{1}{16}.
$$

negatives.text:
If $a$, $b$, $c$ are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\frac{a-b}{a+b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-a}{a+c} < \frac{1}{4}.
$$

If $a$, $b$, $c$ are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\frac{a-b}{a-b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-a}{a+c} < \frac{1}{16}.
$$

If $a$, $b$, $c$ are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\frac{a+b}{a-b} + \frac{b+c}{b-c} + \frac{c+a}{c-a} < \frac{1}{16}.
$$

positive_text: Prove that the equation $2 x^{2} - 3 x + 1 = 3 y^{2} + y$ has infinitely many positive integer solutions.

negatives.text: Show that there are infinitely many solutions in positive integers to $2 a^{2} + 3 a + 1 = 3 b^{2} + b$.
Show that there are infinitely many solutions in positive integers to $2 a^{2} - 3 a + 1 = 3 b^{2} - b$.
Show that there are infinitely many solutions in positive integers to $2 a^{2} - 3 a + 1 = 3 b^{2} + b + 1$.

positive_text: Let $ g $ be a function defined on $ [0,1] $ such that $ g(0) = 0 $, $ g(x/3) = g(x)/2 $, and $ g(1-x) = 1 - g(x) $. Compute $ g\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.

negatives.text: Let $ f $ be a function defined on $ [0,1] $ such that $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f(x/3) = f(x) + 1 $, and $ f(1-x) = 1 - f(x) $. Find $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.

positive_text: Let $g(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \dfrac{b_{i}}{x + b_{i}}$, where $b_{i}$ are distinct positive real numbers. Determine the total length of the domain where $g(x) \geq 1$.

negatives.text: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{a_{1}}{x^2 + a_{1}} + \dfrac{a_{2}}{x^2 + a_{2}} + \ldots + \dfrac{a_{n}}{x^2 + a_{n}}$, where $a_{i}$ are unequal positive reals. Find the sum of the lengths of the intervals in which $f(x) \geq 1$.

Let $f(x) = \dfrac{a_{1}}{x - a_{1}} + \dfrac{a_{2}}{x - a_{2}} + \ldots + \dfrac{a_{n}}{x - a_{n}}$, where $a_{i}$ are unequal positive reals. Find the sum of the lengths of the intervals in which $f(x) \geq 1$.

positive_text: Suppose $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle of side $2$. Demonstrate that for all points $P$ lying on the incircle of triangle $ABC$, the identity $PA^2 + PB^2 + PC^2 = 5$ holds. Furthermore, show that the area of the triangle with sides $PA$, $PB$, and $PC$ is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle with side length $2$. Prove that for any point $P$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, the sum $PA^2 + PB^2 + PC^2 = 5$. Also, show that the triangle formed with side lengths $PA$, $PB$, and $PC$ has area $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$.

positive_text: Let $x_{n}, y_{n}$ be integer sequences defined by: (1) $x_{0}=0$, $y_{0}=8$; (2) $x_{n+2}=2 x_{n+1}-x_{n}+2$, $y_{n+2}=2 y_{n+1}-y_{n}$, and (3) $x_{n}^{2} + y_{n}^{2}$ is a perfect square for $n > 0$. Find two distinct pairs $(x_{1992}, y_{1992})$.

negatives.text: Let $a_{n}, b_{n}$ be integer sequences defined by: $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$; $a_{n+2}=2 a_{n+1}-a_{n}-2$, $b_{n+2}=2 b_{n+1}-b_{n}$; and $a_{n}^{2} + b_{n}^{2}$ is a square for $n > 0$. Find at least two values of $(a_{1992}, b_{1992})$.

Let $a_{n}, b_{n}$ be integer sequences defined by: $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$; $a_{n+2}=2 a_{n+1}-a_{n}+2$, $b_{n+2}=2 b_{n+1}-b_{n}$; and $a_{n}^{2} + b_{n}^{2}$ is a square for $n < 0$. Find at least two values of $(a_{1992}, b_{1992})$.

Let $a_{n}, b_{n}$ be integer sequences defined by: $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$; $a_{n+2}=2 a_{n+1}-a_{n}+2$, $b_{n+2}=2 b_{n+1}-b_{n}$; and $a_{n}^{2} + b_{n}^{2}$ is a cube for $n > 0$. Find at least two values of $(a_{1992}, b_{1992})$.

positive_text: Construct a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$, the distance between $AB$ and $CD$ equal to $h$, and the sum of the lengths of $AB$ and $CD$ equal to $m$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be given. Place $A'$ on the ray $BA$ beyond $A$ so that $AA' = BC$, and place $A''$ on the ray $CA$ beyond $A$ so that $AA'' = BC$. positive_text: Determine all strictly increasing functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that $f(y f(x)) = x^{2} f(xy)$ for all positive integers $x$ and $y$.

negatives.text: Find all strictly increasing functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that $f(y f(x)) = x f(xy)$ for all positive integers $x$ and $y$.
Find all strictly increasing functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that $f(y f(x)) = x^{2} f(x) f(y)$ for all positive integers $x$ and $y$.

positive_text: \text{Let } \triangle ABC \text{ be equilateral. Points D and E lie on AB and AC respectively, and the segment DE is tangent to the incircle of } \triangle ABC. \text{ Prove that } \frac{AD}{DB} + \frac{AE}{EC} = 1.

positive_text: \text{\textit{ABCD}} is a cyclic quadrilateral. A circle with center on \text{\textit{AB}} is tangent to the sides \text{\textit{BC}}, \text{\textit{CD}}, and \text{\textit{DA}}. Prove that \text{\textit{AB}} = \text{\textit{AD}} + \text{\textit{BC}}. Find the maximum possible area of \text{\textit{ABCD}} in terms of \text{\textit{|AB|}} and \text{\textit{|CD|}}.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and let the incircle touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$, and $F$ respectively. Suppose the segment $AD$ intersects the incircle again at a point $X$ such that $AX = XD$. Let $BX$ intersect the incircle again at $Y$, and $CX$ intersect it again at $Z$. Prove that the segments $EY$ and $FZ$ are equal in length.

negatives.text: The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $X$ and $AX = 2XD$. $BX$ meets the circle again at $Y$ and $CX$ meets the circle again at $Z$. Show that $EY = FZ$.

The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $X$ and $AX = XD$. $BY$ meets the circle again at $X$ and $CX$ meets the circle again at $Z$. Show that $EY = FZ$.

The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $X$ and $AX = XD$. $BX$ meets the circle again at $Y$ and $CX$ meets the circle again at $Z$. Show that $EY < FZ$.

positive_text: Let \mathrm{ABC} be a triangle with \mathrm{D} the midpoint of \mathrm{BC}, and let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of \mathrm{AD}. The ray \mathrm{BM} intersects \mathrm{AC} at N. Prove that the condition for \mathrm{AB} to be tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} is that \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{2}.

negatives.text: \mathrm{M} is the midpoint of the median \mathrm{AD} of triangle \mathrm{ABC}. The ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} iff \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BN} / \mathrm{BC})^{2}.

\mathrm{M} is the midpoint of the median \mathrm{AD} of triangle \mathrm{ABC}. The ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} iff \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BA})^{2}.

\mathrm{M} is the midpoint of the median \mathrm{AD} of triangle \mathrm{ABC}. The ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} iff \mathrm{BM}^{2} / \mathrm{BN}^{2} = (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{2}.

positive_text: Let $ n = k^2 - k + 1 $, with $ k = p + 1 $ and $ p $ a prime. Prove that it is possible to place black squares on an $ n \times n $ grid such that each row and column contains exactly $ k $ black squares, and no four black squares form the corners of a rectangle with sides parallel to the grid edges.

negatives.text: Let $ n = k^2 + k + 1 $, where $ k $ is a prime plus one. Show that we can color some squares of an $ n \times n $ board black so that each row and column has exactly $ k $ black squares, but there is no rectangle with sides parallel to the sides of the board which has its four corner squares black.

Let $ n = k^2 - k + 1 $, where $ k $ is a prime plus one. Show that we can color some squares of an $ n \times n $ board black so that each row and column has at most $ k $ black squares, and there is no rectangle with sides parallel to the sides of the board which has its four corner squares black.

Let $ n = k^2 - k + 1 $, where $ k $ is a prime plus one. Show that we can color some squares of an $ n \times n $ board black so that each row and column has exactly $ k $ black squares, and there is no square of size $ 2 \times 2 $ with all four squares black.

positive_text: \text{Suppose } k \geq 1 \text{ is a real number with the property that for all integers } m, n \text{ with } m \equiv 0 \pmod{n}, \text{ we have } \lfloor mk \rfloor \equiv 0 \pmod{\lfloor nk \rfloor}. \text{ Prove that } k \text{ is an integer.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } k \geq 1 \text{ be a real number such that if } m \text{ is a multiple of } n, \text{ then } \lceil mk \rceil \text{ is a multiple of } \lceil nk \rceil. \text{ Show that } k \text{ is an integer.}

\text{Let } k \geq 1 \text{ be a real number such that if } m \text{ is a multiple of } n, \text{ then } \lfloor mk \rfloor + 1 \text{ is a multiple of } \lfloor nk \rfloor + 1. \text{ Show that } k \text{ is an integer.}

\text{Let } k \geq 1 \text{ be a real number such that if } m \text{ is a multiple of } n, \text{ then } \lfloor mk \rfloor^2 \text{ is a multiple of } \lfloor nk \rfloor^2. \text{ Show that } k \text{ is an integer.}

positive_text: \text{Let } n > 1 \text{ be an integer. Let } D_n \text{ be the set of integer coordinate points } (x, y) \text{ such that } |x|, |y| \leq n. \text{ Suppose that each point of } D_n \text{ is assigned one of three colors. Prove that there exist two points of the same color such that the line connecting them contains no other points of } D_n. \text{ Moreover, show that it is possible to assign four colors to the points of } D_n \text{ such that any line containing exactly two points of } D_n \text{ has points of different colors.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } n > 1 \text{ be an integer. Let } D_n \text{ be the set of lattice points } (x, y) \text{ with } |x|, |y| \leq n. \text{ If the points of } D_n \text{ are colored with three colors (one for each point), show that there are always two points with the same color such that the line containing them contains exactly one other point of } D_n. \text{ Show that it is possible to color the points of } D_n \text{ with four colors (one for each point) so that if any line contains two points of } D_n \text{ then those two points have different colors.}

\text{Let } n > 1 \text{ be an integer. Let } D_n \text{ be the set of lattice points } (x, y) \text{ with } |x|, |y| \leq n. \text{ If the points of } D_n \text{ are colored with three colors (one for each point), show that there are always two points with the same color such that the line connecting them has more than one point of } D_n. \text{ Show that it is possible to color the points of } D_n \text{ with four colors (one for each point) so that any line with exactly two points of } D_n \text{ has points of different colors.}

positive_text: Let $o(n)$ be the number of $2n$-tuples $(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}, y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n})$ such that each $x_{i}, y_{j} = 0$ or $1$ and $x_{1} y_{1} + x_{2} y_{2} + \ldots + x_{n} y_{n}$ is odd. Similarly, let $e(n)$ be the number for which the sum is even. Prove that $\dfrac{o(n)}{e(n)} = \dfrac{2^{n} - 1}{2^{n} + 1}$.

negatives.text: Let $o(n)$ be the number of $2n$-tuples $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n})$ such that each $a_{i}, b_{j} = 0$ or $1$ and $a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + \ldots + a_{n} b_{n}$ is odd. Similarly, let $e(n)$ be the number for which the sum is even. Show that $\dfrac{o(n)}{e(n)} = \dfrac{2^{n} + 1}{2^{n} - 1}$.

Let $o(n)$ be the number of $2n$-tuples $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n})$ such that each $a_{i}, b_{j} = 0$ or $1$ and $a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + \ldots + a_{n} b_{n}$ is odd. Similarly, let $e(n)$ be the number for which the sum is even. Show that $\dfrac{o(n)}{e(n)} = \dfrac{2^{n} - 1}{2^{n} - 1}$.

positive_text: Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Suppose $AD$ intersects the incircle again at $Q$. Prove that the line through $E$ and $Q$ contains the midpoint of segment $AF$ if and only if triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AC = BC$.

negatives.text: The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$ iff $AC = BC$.
The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $FQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AC = BC$.
The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AB = BC$.

positive_text: Delegates from $n > 1$ distinct nations are seated in a circle. If two individuals are from the same nation, then the person to the immediate right of each must be from a different nation. Determine the largest possible total number of delegates for each $n$.

negatives.text: Representatives from $n > 1$ different countries sit around a table. If two people are from the same country, then both their respective right and left hand neighbors are from different countries. Find the maximum number of people who can sit at the table for each $n$.

Representatives from $n > 1$ different countries sit around a table. If two people are from the same country, then their respective right hand neighbors are from the same country. Find the maximum number of people who can sit at the table for each $n$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $k < 1000$ for which $k^2$ equals the cube of the sum of the digits in $k$.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the square of the sum of the digits of $n$ equals $n^{2}$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the cube of the product of the digits of $n$ equals $n^{2}$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the cube of the sum of the digits of $n$ equals $n$.

positive_text: Let $P$ be a regular $n$-gon with vertices labeled $1$ to $n > 3$. Connect all pairs of non-adjacent vertices. Prove that when $n$ is odd, it is possible to assign each edge or diagonal a distinct label from $1$ to $n$ such that no label coincides with the labels of its two endpoints and each vertex is incident to edges with distinct labels.

negatives.text: Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is even then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ different from the labels of its endpoints so that at each vertex the sides and diagonals all have different labels.

Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is odd then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ equal to the labels of its endpoints so that at each vertex the sides and diagonals all have different labels.

Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is odd then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ different from the labels of its endpoints so that at each vertex the sides and diagonals all have the same label.

positive_text: Determine all integer solutions $ (n, x, y) $ with $ n, x, y > 1 $ satisfying $ n^x = (n-1)^y + 1 $.

negatives.text: Find all solutions to $ (m+1)^a = m^b - 1 $ in integers greater than $1$.
Find all solutions to $ (m+1)^a = (m^b)^2 + 1 $ in integers greater than $1$.
Find all solutions to $ (m+1)^a = m^b + 2 $ in integers greater than $1$.

positive_text: Define the sequence $b_{n}$ by $b_{1} = 56$ and $b_{n+1} = b_{n} - \frac{1}{b_{n}}$. Prove that $b_{n} < 0$ for some $n$ satisfying $1 \leq n \leq 2001$.

negatives.text: The sequence $a_{n}$ is defined as follows: $a_{1} = 56$, $a_{n+1} = a_{n} + \frac{1}{a_{n}}$. Show that $a_{n} < 0$ for some $n$ such that $0 < n < 2002$.
The sequence $a_{n}$ is defined as follows: $a_{1} = 56$, $a_{n+1} = a_{n} - \frac{1}{a_{n}^2}$. Show that $a_{n} < 0$ for some $n$ such that $0 < n < 2002$.
The sequence $a_{n}$ is defined as follows: $a_{1} = 56$, $a_{n+1} = a_{n} - \frac{1}{a_{n}}$. Show that $a_{n} > 0$ for all $n$ such that $0 < n < 2002$.

positive_text: Suppose $P$ and $Q$ are two sequences of $N$ consecutive integers. Given $N=2003$, is it possible to match each element of $P$ with an element of $Q$ to create $N$ pairs $(p,q)$ such that the sum of each pair results in $N$ consecutive integers? What if $N=2004$?

negatives.text: Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the products of the pairs are $N$ consecutive integers? What about $N=2004$?

Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the differences of the pairs are $N$ consecutive integers? What about $N=2004$?

Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the sums of the pairs are $N$ consecutive even integers? What about $N=2004$?

positive_text:
Find integer solutions $a, b, c$:
$$
a+b=1-c, \quad a^{3}+b^{3}=1-c^{2}
$$

negatives.text:
Solve for integers $x, y, z$:
$$
x+y=1+z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1-z^{2}
$$

Solve for integers $x, y, z$:
$$
x+y=1-z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1+z^{2}
$$

Solve for integers $x, y, z$:
$$
x+y=1-z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1-z^{3}
$$

positive_text: \text{If } p, q, r, t \text{ are real numbers with } p q r \neq 0 \text{ and } \frac{t q + (1 - t) r}{p} = \frac{t r + (1 - t) p}{q} = \frac{t p + (1 - t) q}{r} \text{ then prove that either } p + q + r = 0 \text{ or } p = q = r.

negatives.text: \text{If } a, b, c, x \text{ are real numbers such that } abc \neq 0 \text{ and } \frac{x b - (1 - x) c}{a} = \frac{x c - (1 - x) a}{b} = \frac{x a - (1 - x) b}{c} \text{ then prove that either } a + b + c = 0 \text{ or } a = b = c.

\text{If } a, b, c, x \text{ are real numbers such that } abc \neq 0 \text{ and } \frac{x b + (1 - x) c^2}{a} = \frac{x c + (1 - x) a^2}{b} = \frac{x a + (1 - x) b^2}{c} \text{ then prove that either } a + b + c = 0 \text{ or } a = b = c.

\text{If } a, b, c, x \text{ are real numbers such that } abc \neq 0 \text{ and } \frac{x b + (1 - x) c}{a} < \frac{x c + (1 - x) a}{b} < \frac{x a + (1 - x) b}{c} \text{ then prove that either } a + b + c = 0 \text{ or } a = b = c.

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = CD$, $(\sqrt{3}+1)BC = DA$, and $\angle CDA - \angle DAB = 30^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle ABC - \angle BCD = 90^\circ
$$

negatives.text:
In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}-1)QR = SP$, and $\angle RSP - \angle SPQ = 30^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}+1)QR = SP$, and $\angle SPQ - \angle RSP = 30^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}+1)QR = SP$, and $\angle RSP - \angle SPQ = 60^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

positive_text: Suppose $p, q, r$ are real numbers satisfying $1 \geq p \geq q \geq r \geq 0$. If $\mu$ is a root of the cubic polynomial $x^{3}+p x^{2}+q x+r=0$ (real or complex), show that $|\mu| \leq 1$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be three real numbers such that $1 \geq a \geq b \geq c \geq 0$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x-c=0$ (real or complex), then $|\lambda| \leq 1$.
Let $a, b, c$ be three real numbers such that $1 \geq a \geq b \geq c \geq 0$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+c=0$ (real or complex), then $|\lambda| < 1$.

positive_text:
Let $g(n)$ represent the number of distinct integer-sided triangles with total perimeter $n$ where $n$ is a natural number and $n \geq 3$ (e.g., $g(3)=1$, $g(4)=0$, $g(7)=2$). Prove that

a. $g(1999) > g(1996)$

b. $g(2000) = g(1997)$.

negatives.text:
Let $f(n)$ denote the number of non-congruent integer-sided triangles with perimeter $n$ (e.g., $f(3)=1$, $f(4)=0$, $f(7)=2$). Show that

a. $f(1999) < f(1996)$

b. $f(2000) = f(1997)$.

Let $f(n)$ denote the number of non-congruent integer-sided triangles with perimeter $n$ (e.g., $f(3)=1$, $f(4)=0$, $f(7)=2$). Show that

a. $f(1999) > f(1996)$

b. $f(2000) = f(1996)$.

Let $f(n)$ denote the number of non-congruent integer-sided triangles with perimeter $n$ (e.g., $f(3)=1$, $f(4)=0$, $f(7)=2$). Show that

a. $f(1999) > f(1996)$

b. $f(2000) = f(1997) + 1$.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbf{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{R}$ such that
$$
f(a+b) = f(a) f(b) f(ab)
$$
for every $a, b \in \mathbf{R}$.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbf{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{R}$ such that
$$
f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) + f(xy)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbf{R}$.

Let $\mathbf{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{R}$ such that
$$
f(x+y) = f(x) f(y) f(xy^2)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbf{R}$.

Let $\mathbf{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{R}$ such that
$$
f(x+y) = f(x) f(y) f(x y) + 1
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbf{R}$.

positive_text: Suppose $a, b > 0$ and $a + b = 2$. Show that $$a^{3} b^{3} (a^{3} + b^{3}) \leq 2$$

negatives.text: Let $x, y$ be positive reals such that $x + y = 2$. Prove that $$x^{3} y^{3} (x^{2} + y^{2}) \leq 2$$
Let $x, y$ be positive reals such that $x + y = 2$. Prove that $$x^{3} y^{3} (x^{3} - y^{3}) \leq 2$$
Let $x, y$ be positive reals such that $x + y = 2$. Prove that $$x^{3} y^{3} (x^{3} + y^{3}) < 2$$

positive_text:
Let $PQR$ be a triangle with side lengths $x, y, z$. Define a new triangle $P_1 Q_1 R_1$ with side lengths $x + \frac{y}{2}$, $y + \frac{z}{2}$, and $z + \frac{x}{2}$. Prove that
$$
[P_1 Q_1 R_1] \geq \frac{9}{4}[PQR].
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with sides $a, b, c$. Consider a triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides equal to $a - \frac{b}{2}$, $b - \frac{c}{2}$, $c - \frac{a}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[ABC].
$$

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with sides $a, b, c$. Consider a triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides equal to $a + b$, $b + c$, $c + a$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[ABC].
$$

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with sides $a, b, c$. Consider a triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides equal to $a + \frac{b}{2}$, $b + \frac{c}{2}$, $c + \frac{a}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \leq \frac{9}{4}[ABC].
$$

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, and let $K, L, M, N$ be the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Given that
(i) the diagonal $BD$ bisects the segment $KM$ at a point $Q$;
(ii) the distances from $Q$ to each vertex satisfy $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(iii) the ratio $\frac{LK}{LM}$ equals $\frac{CD}{CB}$,
prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, with midpoints $K, L, M, N$ on $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Suppose
(a) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at $Q$;
(b) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(c) $\frac{LK}{LM} = \frac{CB}{CD}$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, with midpoints $K, L, M, N$ on $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Suppose
(a) $AC$ bisects $KM$ at $Q$;
(b) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(c) $\frac{LK}{LM} = \frac{CD}{CB}$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

positive_text: Let $\beta$ be the real root of the polynomial $x^{5}-x^{3}+x-2=0$. Show that the floor of $\beta^{6}$ is 3.

negatives.text: If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5}-x^{3}-x-2=0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{6}\right]=3$.
If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5}-x^{3}+x-2=0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{7}\right]=3$.
If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5}-x^{3}+x-2=0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{6}\right]=2$.

positive_text:
Let $R$ be the set of all 6-tuples $(p, q, r, s, t, u)$ of positive integers satisfying $p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}+s^{2}+t^{2}=u^{2}$. Define the set
$$
U=\{p q r s t u:(p, q, r, s, t, u) \in R\}
$$
Determine the greatest common divisor of all elements in $U$.

negatives.text:
Let $S$ denote the set of all 6-tuples $(a, b, c, d, e, f)$ of positive integers such that $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2}=f^{2}+1$. Consider the set
$$
T=\{a b c d e f:(a, b, c, d, e, f) \in S\}
$$
Find the greatest common divisor of all the members of $T$.

Let $S$ denote the set of all 6-tuples $(a, b, c, d, e, f)$ of positive integers such that $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2}=f^{2}$ and $a < b < c < d < e$. Consider the set
$$
T=\{a b c d e f:(a, b, c, d, e, f) \in S\}
$$
Find the greatest common divisor of all the members of $T$.

Let $S$ denote the set of all 6-tuples $(a, b, c, d, e, f)$ of positive integers such that $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2}+f^{2}=1$. Consider the set
$$
T=\{a b c d e f:(a, b, c, d, e, f) \in S\}
$$
Find the greatest common divisor of all the members of $T$.

positive_text: Determine all functions $ g: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} $ such that $$ g\left(a^{2} + b g(c)\right) = a g(a) + c g(b) $$ for all $ a, b, c $ in $ \mathbf{R} $.

negatives.text: Find all functions $ f: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} $ such that $$ f\left(x^{2} + y f(z)\right) = x f(x) - z f(y) $$ for all $ x, y, z $ in $ \mathbf{R} $.
Find all functions $ f: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} $ such that $$ f\left(x^{2} + y f(z)\right) = x f(x) + f(z) f(y) $$ for all $ x, y, z $ in $ \mathbf{R} $.
Find all functions $ f: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} $ such that $$ f\left(x^{2} + y f(z)\right) = x f(x) + z f(y) $$ for all $ x, y, z $ in $ \mathbf{R} $ with $ x, y, z > 0 $.

positive_text: Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique pair $(x, y)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(x + y - 1)(x + y - 2) + x $$

negatives.text: Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) + b $$
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b)(a + b - 1) + a $$
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) - a $$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $\gamma$ be a circle tangent to $BC$ at a point moving toward $B$. Prove that if $\gamma$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ from the inside, then it is also tangent to the line from $A$ perpendicular to $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of $ABC$ moves (slides) on $BC$ in the direction of $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ externally, it also touches the altitude through $A$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of $ABC$ moves (slides) on $BC$ in the direction of $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ internally, it also touches the median from $A$ to $BC$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of $ABC$ moves (slides) on $BC$ in the direction of $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ internally, it also touches the angle bisector from $A$.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for all real numbers $ a, b $, the identity
$$
 f(a+b) + f(a)f(b) = (1+b)f(a) + (1+a)f(b) + f(ab)
$$
holds.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) - f(xy),
$$
for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $.

Find all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) + f(x)f(y),
$$
for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $.

Find all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) + f(x^2 + y^2),
$$
for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $.

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n = x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}$, where $x, y, z$ are positive integers. Show that
$$
9 n = (s_{1} x + t_{1} y + u_{1} z)^{2} + (s_{2} x + t_{2} y + u_{2} z)^{2} + (s_{3} x + t_{3} y + u_{3} z)^{2}
$$
for some nonzero integers $s_{j}$, $t_{j}$, $u_{j}$. Additionally, if $3$ does not divide at least one of $x, y, z$, prove that $9 n$ can be written as $p^{2} + q^{2} + r^{2}$, where $p, q, r$ are positive integers and none of them is divisible by $3$.

negatives.text:
Let $n$ be a natural number such that $n = a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}$, for some natural numbers $a, b, c$. Prove that
$$
9 n = (p_{1} a + q_{1} b + r_{1} c)^{2} + (p_{2} a + q_{2} b + r_{2} c)^{2} + (p_{3} a + q_{3} b + r_{3} c)^{2}
$$
